A 23-hour-old girl is evaluated for jaundice in the newborn nursery. The infant was born at term via cesarean delivery to a 33-year-old mother,
gravida 2 para 2. The pregnancy was complicated by systemic lupus erythematosus and end-stage renal disease, for which the mother received
regular hemodialysis. The delivery was complicated by intraamniotic infection and arrest of labor, necessitating cesarean delivery. Apgar scores
were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The infant was prescribed ampicillin and cefotaxime shortly after delivery. The patient is
exclusively breastfeeding and has lost 3% of her body weight. She has urinated twice and stooled once. Physical examination shows jaundice on
the face and upper trunk but is otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory results are as follows:
Serum chemistry
Sodium
142 mEq/L
Potassium
3.8 mEq/L
Creatinine
4.2 mg/dL
Liver function studies
Total bilirubin 4.3 mg/dL
Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's elevated creatinine level?
questions.explanation:
A serum creatinine level is an effective marker of kidney disease in adults; however, in neonates, the creatinine level is often a reflection of the
maternal level because creatinine freely crosses the placenta. In healthy term infants, creatinine levels decrease rapidly over the first 2 postnatal
weeks to a nadir reflective of infant muscle mass. Therefore, a creatinine level is often a suboptimal determinate of kidney disease; however,
these levels are often drawn as part of the sepsis workup, such as in this neonate, and require additional evaluation.
In these cases, the first step in evaluation includes assessment of oliguria (normal urine output is at least one void per day of life), edema, and
hypertension, which would suggest renal disease. Patients with any of these signs require possible renal ultrasound and additional laboratory
evaluation (eg, trending serum creatinine), particularly if there are risk factors for renal injury (eg, nephrotoxic medications, perinatal hypoxia).
This neonate's normal urine output and unremarkable physical examination (eg, normotensive, expected weight loss) suggest normal kidneys.
Therefore, the serum creatinine level is reflective of the mother's creatinine level from renal failure.
(Choice A) In cases of bilateral renal agenesis, serum creatinine rises abnormally after birth; however, no or minimal urine output is expected
(this patient has voided twice). In addition, patients typically have respiratory distress (secondary to pulmonary hypoplasia) and other findings of
Potter sequence (eg, flat nose, limb deformities).
(Choices B and C) Breastfeeding jaundice occurs due to inadequate fluid intake while breastfeeding is being established and often indicates
relative dehydration, which can lead to prerenal, acute kidney injury. Although this patient has mild jaundice, there is no evidence of dehydration
(eg, adequate urine output, expected weight loss from birthweight [<10%]), and bilirubin is normal for age.
(Choice D) Hypoxic-ischemic renal injury results from a perinatal insult, leading to an abnormally elevated serum creatinine; however, this infant's
normal Apgar scores (8 and 9) and examination make perinatal asphyxia unlikely.
Educational objective:
Serum creatinine at birth is equivalent to the serum creatinine of the mother because creatinine passes across the placenta. In healthy term
infants, creatinine normalizes over the first 2 weeks of life to a nadir that reflects neonatal muscle mass.

This patient has primary hypothyroidism (ie, low free thyroxine [T4], high TSH) associated with an elevated prolactin level. Both hypothyroidism
and hyperprolactinemia (individually or in conjunction) can cause central hypogonadism, manifesting with menstrual abnormalities and
infertility, via multiple mechanisms:
• Hypothyroidism causes decreased responsiveness of the pituitary to GnRH, leading to decreased gonadotropin (ie, FSH, LH) secretion.
• Thyrotropin-releasing hormone, which is upregulated in hypothyroidism, stimulates the pituitary secretion of prolactin.
• Hyperprolactinemia, whether due to hypothyroidism or as an isolated disorder, further suppresses gonadotropin secretion.
In addition to mild to moderate hyperprolactinemia (serum prolactin <100 ng/mL), laboratory findings in patients with hypothyroid-related
hypogonadism include low FSH and LH and low serum estradiol (low testosterone in men).
When patients have primary hypothyroidism and hyperprolactinemia, the thyroid disorder is usually the primary condition; hyperprolactinemia does
not cause hypothyroidism. Therefore, levothyroxine therapy should be initiated first, which usually corrects prolactin levels and restores
reproductive function. However, if prolactin levels are unusually high (ie, ≥100 ng/dL) or do not normalize with the treatment of hypothyroidism,
prolactinoma should be suspected and may require cranial imaging (ie, MRI) and dopamine agonist (eg, cabergoline) therapy (Choices A and D).
(Choice C) Although a small amount of T3 is released from the thyroid, T3 is generated primarily by deiodination of T4 in peripheral tissues.
Serum T3 levels are useful in evaluating hyperthyroidism but not primary hypothyroidism.

evaluation of central precocious puberty. This patient's gonadotropin abnormalities are due to primary hypothyroidism, so a GnRH stimulation test
would not be helpful.
Educational objective:
Menstrual irregularities (eg, irregular menses, infertility) are common in hypothyroidism. Typical laboratory findings include elevated prolactin and
low FSH and LH levels with low serum estradiol (low testosterone in men). Reproductive function usually normalizes with levothyroxine therapy.

This patient with conjunctival injection with discharge has acute conjunctivitis, which is typically viral, bacterial, or allergic. This patient's watery
discharge and concomitant fever, rhinorrhea, and sore throat are suggestive of viral conjunctivitis.
Viral conjunctivitis is highly contagious, and outbreaks are common in facilities with close contact (eg, day care, school). Ocular symptoms include
diffuse conjunctival injection that may be unilateral or bilateral and watery or mucoid discharge. The tarsal conjunctiva, which lines the
inner eyelid, may have a follicular appearance due to the presence of lymphocyte aggregates, as seen in this case; patients may describe a
gritty or burning sensation. Prodromal symptoms (eg, rhinorrhea, sore throat) are often present.
The diagnosis of viral conjunctivitis is clinical. Treatment, including cool, moist compresses and artificial tears as a lubricant, is supportive. The
condition is self-limited and typically resolves within 2 weeks. Because transmission is via direct contact with infected secretions, prevention is
achieved by washing the hands frequently and sanitizing contaminated surfaces.
(Choice B) Oral valacyclovir is used in the treatment of herpes simplex keratitis, a corneal infection that causes pain, decreased visual acuity, and
photophobia with dendritic lesions and ulcers on examination. None of these features are present in this patient.
(Choice C) Topical olopatadine is an antihistamine and mast cell-stabilizing agent primarily indicated for allergic conjunctivitis. Although
conjunctival injection, watery discharge, and a follicular appearance of the tarsal conjunctivae are typical, bilateral symptoms and marked ocular
pruritus would be expected but are not seen in this patient.
(Choice D) Topical polymyxin-trimethoprim is used to treat bacterial conjunctivitis, which presents with thick, purulent discharge, unlike this
patient's watery discharge. In addition, follicular conjunctivitis of the tarsal conjunctivae is not typically seen in bacterial conjunctivitis.
(Choice E) Topical prednisone is used in the treatment of ocular inflammatory conditions, such as uveitis. Redness of the eye can occur, but
ocular pain and/or reduced visual acuity would be expected, and profuse watery discharge is not typical. Topical glucocorticoids are not generally
indicated for acute viral conjunctivitis due to potential risks (eg, corneal scarring).
Educational objective:
Acute viral conjunctivitis is a self-limited condition that typically presents with diffuse conjunctival injection, watery discharge, and a gritty
sensation. The diagnosis is clinical, and treatment is supportive, including cool, moist compresses and artificial tears.

questions.prompt:
A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her father due to "strange behavior." Earlier that day, the patient insisted that a
television newscaster was talking directly to her about the risks of "poison rays" from the moon. Her father says that she has "not been herself" for
the past year. He is upset about her declining grades, along with increasing conflicts with her younger siblings and social isolation from her
friends. A month ago, the patient abruptly quit the part-time job that she had previously enjoyed because she believed that her coworkers were
spying on her. In the emergency department, she is agitated and the decision is made to admit her to the psychiatric unit. After a comprehensive
evaluation, the patient is diagnosed with schizophrenia. She is stabilized on risperidone over a period of 3 weeks, and discharge plans to return
home are discussed. Her father asks what can be done to decrease the likelihood of rehospitalization. In addition to maintaining risperidone,
which of the following measures would be most helpful for this patient?

options.label: Encourage the patient to resume employment
Encourage the patient to return to school immediately
Recommend close supervision of the patient at al times

questions.explanation:
Although antipsychotic medication is the primary treatment for schizophrenia, integrating psychosocial interventions into a broader treatment
program can improve outcomes. Family interventions, including psychoeducation and family therapy, have proved to be high-yield interventions
in schizophrenia that reduce the risk of rehospitalization.
Family intervention consists of a collaborative process that educates the patient and family about the symptoms and course of schizophrenia with
the goal of reducing family stress and conflict (eg, educating the family that the patient's social isolation and declining grades are not "laziness";
they are negative symptoms of schizophrenia). Patients with schizophrenia who have critical, hostile, or overinvolved family members have a
higher risk of relapse; patients in a home atmosphere that is stable and supportive, with family stressors kept to a minimum, have a decreased
risk of relapse.
(Choice A) Employment can help provide a sense of purpose and worth; however, asking this patient to resume employment shortly after a
psychotic episode in which she felt paranoid about her coworkers would be unnecessarily stressful and could increase the risk of relapse.
Structured employment programs that provide on-the-job support can be helpful for patients with serious mental illness.
(Choice B) Although returning to school would provide structure and goals for this patient, she is unlikely to be successful immediately after a
psychotic episode. A gradual return with a reduced schedule would be a more appropriate recommendation.
(Choice C) Having family members supervise the patient at all times is likely to be experienced as intrusive and stressful. Overinvolved family-
patient interactions are associated with worse outcomes.
(Choice E) Insight-oriented psychotherapy focuses on uncovering unconscious patterns originating in childhood experiences; it is not indicated
for patients with schizophrenia because it may initially cause increased anxiety that can destabilize those recovering from an acute psychotic
episode. In contrast, cognitive-behavioral therapy, which combines cognitive approaches and social skills training, is a helpful adjunct to
medication in the treatment of schizophrenia.
Educational objective:
Family psychosocial interventions are indicated for patients with a recent psychotic episode who have significant ongoing contact with family
members. Minimizing conflict and stress in the home decreases the risk of relapse in patients with schizophrenia.

This patient likely has hemoperitoneum due to a ruptured ovarian cyst. Ovarian cysts are common in ovulating women of reproductive age

questions.prompt:
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for evaluation of dark brown urine for a day. He has had no fever, dysuria, hesitancy, or urinary frequency.
For the past 3 days, the patient has had rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, and a sore throat, but these symptoms are improving. He has bilateral,
sensorineural hearing loss that has worsened over the past 4 years. A maternal uncle died from complications of a renal transplant 5 years ago.
Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F), blood pressure is 132/94 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 14/min. The abdomen is soft and
nontender and has no palpable masses. There is no suprapubic or costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis reveals hematuria. Serum
creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL, and serum complement levels are normal. A renal biopsy is performed. Which of the following is the most likely histologic
Tinding?

options.label: Linear deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane
Longitudinal splitting of the glomerular basement membrane
Mesangial and glomerular capillary deposition of C3 and IgG

questions.explanation:
Alport syndrome
• Inherited (most commonly X-linked)
Pathogenesis
• Mutation of type IV collagen
• Nephropathy
• Hematuria (microscopic or gross)
• Progressive renal insufficiency
• + Proteinuria
Clinical findings
• + Hypertension
• Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss
• Anterior lenticonus (lens protrusion)
• Molecular genetic testing
Diagnosis
• Renal biopsy: longitudinal splitting of GBM
GBM = glomerular basement membrane.
Alport syndrome is an inherited, progressive disease affecting type IV collagen in the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), cochlea, and
eye. The typical patient is a boy age <10 with gross hematuria after a recent upper respiratory infection, as in this case. Asymptomatic,
microscopic hematuria often precedes gross hematuria, which recurs periodically and may be accompanied by hypertension, proteinuria, and
chronic renal failure. Mutated collagen in the cochlea and eye results in sensorineural hearing loss and anterior lenticonus (conical lens
protrusion), respectively.
Most cases are X-linked, and patients often have a family history of chronic kidney disease, such as the renal transplant in this patient's uncle.
History may also reveal hereditary hearing loss.
Laboratory results may demonstrate elevated serum creatinine and normal complement levels. Diagnosis is confirmed by renal biopsy, with
electron microscopy showing a lamellated GBM due to longitudinal splitting of the lamina densa. Genetic testing can also screen patients with
a family history of Alport syndrome or confirm the diagnosis in a symptomatic patient.
Management is supportive and may include transplant in patients with end-stage renal disease.
(Choice A) Renal biopsy in minimal change disease shows effacement of podocyte foot processes. Patients are classically age <6 with marked
proteinuria but no hematuria, renal insufficiency, or hypertension, making this diagnosis unlikely.
(Choice B) Goodpasture syndrome is a progressive glomerulonephritis accompanied by pulmonary disease (ie, alveolar hemorrhage); biopsy
reveals linear IgG deposition in the GBM. This patient has no pulmonary symptoms, and sensorineural hearing loss is not associated with
Goodpasture syndrome.
(Choice D) Biopsy in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis reveals mesangial and glomerular capillary deposition of C3 and IgG. Patients
typically have edema, hematuria, and hypertension. However, symptoms usually develop 1-3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis or impetigo,
and the C3 level is decreased (not seen in this patient).
(Choice E) IgA nephropathy is characterized by mesangial IgA deposition. Patients have concomitant gross hematuria and upper respiratory
symptoms (eg, rhinorrhea, sore throat). Hypertension and renal insufficiency are rarely seen, and IgA nephropathy is not associated with
sensorineural hearing loss.
Educational objective:
Alport syndrome is a progressive disease that presents with recurrent hematuria in boys age <10, often with a family history of renal failure and/or
hearing loss. Complement levels are normal, and renal biopsy shows longitudinal splitting of the glomerular basement membrane.

This patient who is dressed in multiple layers of clothing (onesies, pajamas) and spends most of the day and night swaddled in a fleece blanket
most likely has miliaria rubra, or heat rash. Infants are prone to miliaria rubra because their eccrine sweat glands within the epidermis are not
fully developed or have delayed patency. As a result, hot or humid environments lead to sweat accumulation within the glands and an
inflammatory reaction.
Clinical manifestations include a fine (2-4 mm), erythematous, papular rash, as seen in this patient. It is typically located in intertriginous areas
(eg, groin, axilla, anterior neck) or in areas where the skin is occluded (eg, back, head) by clothing, hats, or adhesive bandages. The rash is
typically asymptomatic but may be pruritic, and infants are otherwise well appearing.
Management involves avoidance of overbundling and synthetic fabrics and switching to thin clothing made of breathable material (eg, cotton).
Overheating and sweating can also be reduced by creating a cooler environment (eg, air conditioning, fan) when possible. If the rash is severe
or associated with pruritus, topical low/mid-potency corticosteroids may be used as adjunctive therapy.
(Choice A) High-potency topical corticosteroids are not typically recommended in neonates due to the risk of systemic absorption enhanced by
the thin stratum corneum in this age group. Moreover, absorption is further increased when applied to large, occluded areas, as is typically seen
in miliaria rubra.
(Choice B) Topical antihistamines improve histamine-mediated pruritus, such as urticaria. In contrast to this patient's rash, urticaria presents with
raised, erythematous wheals. Moreover, the inflammatory response in miliaria rubra is not histamine mediated.
(Choice C) Cutaneous candidiasis, which can be treated with topical nystatin, usually affects the intertriginous areas, not the back. Moreover, the
rash is characterized by beefy-red plaques with satellite erythematous papules, which are absent in this patient.
(Choice E) Reassurance alone is appropriate for erythema toxicum neonatorum, which classically presents as a maculopapular rash that evolves
into pustules on an erythematous base. This rash develops in the first 2-3 days of life and resolves by age 1 week, which is inconsistent with this
patient's history.
Educational objective:
Miliaria rubra is a fine, erythematous, papular eruption that classically develops in infants exposed to hot or humid environments and affects the
intertriginous areas or areas under occlusion. Management involves avoidance of overheating by use of thin, cotton clothing and placement in a
cool environment when possible.

experienced several episodes of nausea and vomiting this morning. The patient has had gastroesophageal reflux disease throughout the
pregnancy, but the symptoms have rapidly become much worse. During her visit last week, she was fatigued, and her blood pressure was 130/80
mm Hg. Current blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg and pulse is 86/min. BMI is 42 kg/m2. Physical examination shows extreme tenderness to
palpation in the midline and right upper quadrant of the abdomen but absence of peritoneal signs. Fetal heart tones are 130/min using Doppler

A. Cystic duct obstruction
B. Distension of the liver capsule
C. Fatty infiltration of the liver
D. Pancreatic inflammation
) E. Peptic ulcer perforation

HELLP syndrome
• Nausea/vomiting
• Right upper quadrant pain
• Headache
Clinical findings
• Visual changes
• Hypertension
• Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
Laboratory
• Elevated liver enzymes
abnormalities
• Thrombocytopenia
• + Proteinuria
• Delivery
Treatment
• Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis
• Antihypertensives (eg, hydralazine)
• Abruptio placentae
• Subcapsular liver hematoma
• Acute renal failure
Complications
• Pulmonary edema
• Disseminated intravascular coagulation
HELLP = Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelet count.
This pregnant patient with hypertension and right upper quadrant pain likely has preeclampsia with severe features (ie, new hypertension at ≥20
weeks gestation with signs of end-organ damage) and/or HELLP (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) syndrome.
These disorders likely represent a spectrum of disease causing maternal endothelial dysfunction (eg, hypertension, vasospasm). HELLP
syndrome also causes platelet overactivation (ie, thrombocytopenia) and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (ie, anemia with elevated
indirect bilirubin) due to the deposition of platelet-fibrin microthrombi within capillaries.
The liver is commonly affected in HELLP syndrome. Microthrombi deposition in the hepatic portal system results in decreased hepatic perfusion,
liver ischemia, and hepatocellular injury (eg, nausea/vomiting, right upper quadrant pain, elevated transaminases). The gradual distension of
the hepatic [Glisson] capsule causes the classic presentation of worsening right upper quadrant pain without associated peritoneal signs.
Severe cases may progress to liver necrosis and hemorrhage, resulting in a subcapsular hematoma (ie, blood pooling beneath the hepatic
capsule).
(Choice A) Obstruction of the cystic duct (ie, cholelithiasis) may cause right upper quadrant pain and elevated liver transaminases; however,
patients typically have elevated direct (ie, conjugated) bilirubin levels. There is no association with thrombocytopenia or hypertension.
(Choice C) Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) and HELLP syndrome share many features, including hypertension, right upper quadrant pain,
and elevated transaminases. In contrast to HELLP syndrome, which causes indirect hepatocellular injury due to decreased liver perfusion, AFLP
causes fulminant liver failure due to complete fatty infiltration of hepatocytes. Therefore, patients with AFLP typically have jaundice,
encephalopathy, coagulopathy, and profound hypoglycemia.
(Choice D) Lipase and leukocyte count are normal in this patient, making the diagnosis of pancreatitis less likely. In addition, pain associated
with pancreatitis is typically midline and radiates to the back.
(Choice E) Patients with peptic ulcer perforation can have right upper quadrant pain; however, they typically have peritoneal signs (eg, abdominal
rigidity, rebound/guarding) due to intraperitoneal spillage of caustic gastric acid.
(Choice F) Hepatic adenomas are benign liver tumors associated with elevated estrogen (eg, pregnancy, oral contraceptive use). Rupture leads
to brisk intraabdominal bleeding, a possible palpable liver mass, and hemodynamic instability (eg, hypotension, tachycardia).
Educational objective:
HELLP (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets) syndrome can present during pregnancy with worsening right upper quadrant
pain due to gradual distension of the hepatic (Glisson) capsule. Patients may have associated hypertension and proteinuria.

Item 2 of 2
The patient is admitted to the hospital, and an intravenous line and urinary catheter are placed. She receives corticosteroids to accelerate fetal
lung maturity and magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection. Three hours later, the patient develops dyspnea and has a drop in arterial oxygen
saturation. Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 150/80 mm Hg, pulse is 112/min, and respirations are 24/min. Pulse oximetry is
91% on room air. Examination shows bibasilar crackles and use of accessory muscles for breathing. Heart sounds are tachycardic and without
murmur. There is 3+ pitting edema of the lower extremities, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. The remainder of the examination is
normal. Urine output is 60 mL/hr. What is the most likely cause of this patient's respiratory symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Pathophysiology of pulmonary edema
in preeclampsia/eclampsia
T Generalized arterial
vasospasm (systemic
hypertension)
1 Afterload against which
the heart is pumping
1 Pulmonary capillary
pressure
1 Albumin
J Renal function
Pulmonary edema
1 Vascular permeability

This patient's dyspnea, hypoxia, and bibasilar crackles on examination are most likely due to acute pulmonary edema, a life-threatening
complication of preeclampsia with severe features. Patients with preeclampsia typically have generalized arterial vasospasm, leading to
increased systemic vascular resistance and high cardiac afterload. In response, the heart becomes hyperdynamic to attempt to overcome
the systemic hypertension. This causes increased pulmonary capillary pressure, which drives fluid from the capillaries into the interstitium.
Preeclampsia with severe features predisposes to acute pulmonary edema because it causes endothelial damage, leading to increased capillary
permeability. This increased permeability promotes decreased serum albumin levels and decreased capillary oncotic pressure that enables third
spacing (eg, peripheral pitting edema). In addition, normal diuresis is impeded due to decreased renal function.
Management includes supplemental oxygen, fluid restriction, and diuretic medications in severe cases. Fluid restriction and diuretic medications
are used with caution because patients have overall decreased plasma volume (due to third spacing) and aggressive treatment may compromise
placental perfusion and fetal wellbeing.
(Choice A) Amniotic fluid embolism, caused by amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation, can cause sudden hypoxemic respiratory failure.
However, patients typically develop circulatory collapse with severe hypotension, making this diagnosis less likely.
(Choice B) Bronchospasm may cause dyspnea and hypoxemia, but it usually causes wheezing instead of bibasilar crackles.
(Choice C) Excessive magnesium sulfate can cause neuromuscular depression, resulting in decreased respiratory effort/apnea, muscle
paralysis, and somnolence. Unlike this patient, those with magnesium sulfate toxicity typically have decreased deep tendon reflexes and
decreased respiratory effort.
(Choice D) Peripartum cardiomyopathy can cause left ventricular failure and acute pulmonary edema with bibasilar lung crackles. However,
patients typically have an S3 and murmur (ie, mitral regurgitation) and elevated jugular venous pressure.
(Choice F) The risk for pulmonary embolus is increased peripartum due to the prothrombotic effects of estrogen. Although pulmonary embolism
can cause tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia, it does not typically cause acute bibasilar crackles and is not usually associated with pitting
edema.
Educational objective:
Pulmonary edema is a life-threatening complication of preeclampsia with severe features. It is caused by increased systemic vascular resistance,
capillary permeability, and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure in addition to decreased serum albumin levels.

questions.prompt:
A 4-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department due to not moving her right arm. The patient was behaving and moving normally when
she awoke this morning. The father says he was playfully swinging her by the hands when she suddenly started crying and refused to use her
right arm. They have played like this previously, and it usually makes her laugh. The patient lives with her father and her mother. Physical
examination shows a well-nourished child who holds her right arm extended downward with the forearm pronated and avoids moving it. There is
no bony tenderness to palpation. Several bruises in various stages are noted on the anterior lower legs bilaterally; no bruises or other
abnormalities are seen. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

options.label: Order an x-ray of the right arm
Perform closed reduction and apply a cast

questions.explanation:
Radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow)
• Pull injury in child age 1-4: axial traction on forearm with elbow extended (child pulled, lifted, or swung by arm)
Mechanism
• Annular ligament slips past radial head & becomes trapped in radiohumeral joint
• Arm held with elbow extended & forearm pronated
• Pain with forearm/elbow movement
Physical
• + Mild tenderness over radial head
findings
• No swelling, deformity, or other tenderness
• Reduction: hyperpronation of forearm OR supination of forearm & flexion of elbow → symptom resolution within
minutes
Management
• No postreduction imaging or care required
This 4-year-old child is holding her forearm in pronation and not moving the extremity after being swung by the arms. These findings are
consistent with radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow), a common injury in preschool-aged children.
The mechanism involves axial traction applied to a pronated forearm and extended elbow. Caregivers may report a history of pulling the arm
(eg, to prevent a fall) or lifting or swinging the child by the arm immediately before symptom onset. Traction allows the annular ligament to slip
past the radial head and become trapped in the radiohumeral joint. The child is usually not in distress unless there is an attempt to move the
elbow or forearm, which is characteristically held in a pronated position with the elbow extended, as demonstrated by this patient.
When the mechanism and examination findings are classic and there are no signs of fracture (eg, deformity, swelling), the diagnosis is made
clinically. Treatment is reduction of the annular ligament, first by applying pressure on the radial head and then either hyperpronating the forearm
or supinating the forearm and then flexing the elbow. Successful reduction may produce an audible or palpable click. Normal use of the arm is
expected within minutes after reduction, and no postprocedure interventions (eg, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, cast) are required (Choice
D).
(Choice B) A skeletal survey to assess for healing fractures should be performed when child abuse is suspected, as with an unusual bruising
location (eg, cheek, ears) or an injury that is inconsistent with the reported mechanism. This patient's anterior shin bruises are a normal finding in
a preschool-aged child, and the mechanism of arm injury is classic for radial head subluxation.
(Choice C) X-rays should be obtained if the history is inconsistent with the expected mechanism of radial head subluxation or if signs suggest an
underlying fracture, such as deformity, swelling, or bony tenderness beyond the radial head. This patient exhibits none of these features.

Orthostatic syncope
• Medications (eg, vasodilators, inotropic/chronotropic blockade, diuretics)
Etiologies
• Autonomic dysfunction (eg, advanced age, neurodegenerative disease)
• Hypovolemia (eg, fluid restriction, Gl losses, fever)
• Typically occurs with standing from seated/supine position
Clinical features
• Premonitory symptoms (eg, light-headedness, visual blurring) common
Diagnosis
• ≥20 mm Hg in SBP or ≥10 mm Hg in DBP after standing from supine position
• Modify postural transitions (eg, rise slowly when standing)
Treatment
• Discontinue or dose of exacerbating medications

DBP = diastolic blood pressure; GI = gastrointestinal; SBP = systolic blood pressure.
This patient who had a brief loss of consciousness (LOC) shortly after standing from the wrestling mat most likely experienced syncope due to
orthostatic hypotension (ie, orthostatic syncope).
Orthostatic hypotension occurs when blood pressure is significantly reduced on standing, typically due to hypovolemia or an impaired
baroreceptor-mediated response (eg, autonomic dysfunction). In this patient, the most likely cause is hypovolemia due to fluid restriction and
diuretic use, a method used by some athletes in combat sports (eg, wrestling, boxing) to achieve rapid weight loss and compete in a lighter
weight category. Evidence in this patient includes dry mucous membranes, hemoconcentration, an elevated blood urea nitrogen/creatinine ratio,
and hypokalemia from diuretic-induced potassium elimination.
Standing normally causes a rapid drop in blood pressure due to venous pooling in the lower extremities, triggering a baroreceptor-mediated
increase in sympathetic drive with peripheral vasoconstriction to mobilize blood from the legs, as well as increased heart rate and contractility to
increase cardiac output. In euvolemic patients, sufficient intravascular volume allows an intact baroreceptor-mediated response to maintain
adequate cardiac preload, cardiac output, and cerebral perfusion. However, inadequate intravascular volume prevents the maintenance of
cerebral perfusion, sometimes resulting in syncope.
(Choice A) Inherited conduction abnormalities (eg, congenital long QT syndrome) can cause arrhythmia, leading to syncope. However, warning
symptoms (eg, light-headedness) are usually absent, and ECG is frequently abnormal (eg, prolonged QT interval).

This patient completed appropriate treatment of acute cystitis but continues to have persistent proteinuria. In the context of long-standing
diabetes mellitus, this suggests diabetic nephropathy (DN). DN is characterized by irreversible injury to the glomerular basement membrane
and surrounding structures due to metabolic byproducts (eg, advanced glycation end products, reactive oxygen species) associated with
chronically elevated blood glucose and worsened by excessive intraglomerular pressures.
Regular screening for DN should be performed annually via a random urine albumin/creatinine ratio, starting at either the time of diagnosis (type
2) or 5 years after diagnosis (type 1). Detection of moderately increased albuminuria (ie, albumin/creatinine ratio of 30-300 mg/g) signifies
incipient DN, and the following management strategies should be initiated to prevent progression to overt DN:
• Tight blood pressure control, preferably with either an ACE inhibitor (eg, lisinopril) or angiotensin receptor blocker (eg, losartan)
• Tight glycemic control (eg, hemoglobin A1c <7%), preferably with the use of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (eg, canagliflozin)
and/or glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists (eg, semaglutide)
(Choice A) Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) can be caused by antibiotics (eg, methicillin), infections (eg, Legionella), or systemic disease (eg,
sarcoidosis). Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a potential cause of AIN; however, typical findings include acutely elevated creatinine level,
pyuria, and white blood cell casts.
(Choice B) Atherosclerotic vascular disease can lead to renal artery stenosis, a common cause of secondary and treatment-resistant
hypertension in adults. Patients typically have elevated creatinine levels, but persistent proteinuria is not typical and is more suggestive of DN.
(Choice D) Use of sulfonamide antibiotics can lead to insoluble crystal precipitation in kidney tubules, with subsequent obstruction and acute
kidney injury. However, crystal-induced obstruction would not cause persistent proteinuria; moreover, acute creatinine elevation or crystalluria
would be expected.
(Choice E) In adults, vesicoureteral reflux (ie, retrograde passage of urine into the renal pelvis) is associated with neurogenic bladder and can
cause frequent urinary tract infections. Long-standing diabetes mellitus may cause autonomic bladder dysfunction; however, this patient does not
have associated symptoms of chronic incontinence, and persistent proteinuria would be uncommon.
Educational objective:
Elevated glomerular pressures and oxidative damage to the glomerular basement membrane in long-standing diabetes mellitus can lead to
diabetic nephropathy with persistent proteinuria. Treatment includes tight control of blood pressure (eg, ACE inhibitor) and blood sugar (eg,
sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor, glucagon-like peptide-1 agonist).

the past week. Two days ago, he developed fever and worsening neck pain. Today, the patient has refused to eat or drink. He has no chronic
medical conditions, and immunizations are current. Temperature is 39.7 C (103.5 F), pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 24/min. On
examination, the patient appears tired and uncomfortable. Palpation of the neck reveals bilateral anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. The patient
refuses to move his neck; passive extension is painful. His voice is muffled. Mouth opening is limited by pain, and the tonsils appear
erythematous and symmetrically enlarged with white exudates. The uvula is midline. Chest auscultation reveals good bilateral air entry without
stridor or rhonchi. Lateral neck radiograph is shown in the exhibit. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

• Age 2-4 but can occur in any age group
Epidemiology
• Polymicrobial (group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus &
respiratory anaerobes)

This patient's fever, odynophagia/dysphagia, neck pain with extension, muffled voice, and x-ray findings are concerning for retropharyngeal
abscess (RPA). RPA is a soft-tissue infection of the neck due to polymicrobial bacterial (eg, Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus,
oral anaerobes) infection of the potential space between the pharynx and the vertebral fascia. It is most often preceded by upper respiratory
infection, as in this case, but can also result from direct spread of local bacterial infection (eg, pharyngitis, tonsillitis). RPA occurs most commonly
in children age 2-4. The incidence decreases after age 4 due to retropharyngeal lymph node regression and fewer viral upper respiratory
infections.
On lateral neck x-ray, the prevertebral soft-tissue space is normally narrower than the vertebral bodies; widening of this prevertebral space is
suggestive of RPA. A CT scan with contrast confirms the diagnosis. Large RPAs can obstruct the airway and major vascular structures. Early
diagnosis, appropriate airway management, prompt antimicrobial therapy, and surgical drainage for larger abscesses are essential to prevent
obstructive complications.

questions.prompt:
A 28-year-old man with bipolar I disorder comes to the office for a follow-up visit. He experienced his first manic episode 7 years ago, and the
disorder responded well to lithium. The patient became nonadherent with his medication after his condition improved and then experienced a
second manic episode 9 months later. Over the next 5 years, he experienced 3 additional manic episodes, 2 depressive episodes, and a suicide
attempt. Since his most recent hospitalization for a manic episode 3 years ago, he has remained on lithium and has had no depressive, manic, or
hypomanic signs or symptoms. The patient also has no lithium adverse effects, and levels confirm that he is taking the medication as prescribed.
Today, he inquires about the possibility of discontinuing lithium, adding that he does not want to be dependent on medication and is "in a much
more stable place than before." Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient's condition?

options.label: Discontinue lithium and recommend initiating psychotherapy
Discontinue lithium gradually over the course of 2-4 weeks and initiate valproate
Discontinue lithium gradually over the course of several months
Recommend that the patient continue lithium for an additional year then discontinue gradually

Bipolar I disorder is a mood disorder characterized by ≥1 episodes of mania; it also often includes major depressive episodes. Patients with
severe bipolar I disorder (eg, frequent relapses, suicide attempts, recurrent hospitalizations) require lifelong maintenance pharmacotherapy to
reduce the risk for relapse.
Patients often struggle with the idea of taking medication for life and may want to discontinue maintenance pharmacotherapy for a variety of
reasons (eg, adverse effects, desire to be "medication free," poor illness awareness). However, in most bipolar patients, discontinuing
maintenance treatment leads to a recurrent mood episode within a year. This patient's request to stop medication despite his history of 7 prior
mood episodes, a suicide attempt, and a previous failed discontinuation attempt should cause alarm. In addition, lithium's protective effects
against suicide would be lost.
In patients with limited insight into the dangers of stopping treatment, respect for patient autonomy must be balanced by the physician's
responsibility to act in the best interest of the patient. Nonjudgmental education about realistic concerns for life-damaging consequences (eg,
bankruptcy, incarceration, divorce), suicide, and future treatment resistance should be reinforced. With this patient, ongoing discussion over
multiple sessions, rather than an immediate decision, is recommended. This allows further understanding of and working through this patient's
fear of being "dependent" on medication and avoids an impulsive decision.
(Choices B and D) Stopping medication altogether and/or pursuing psychotherapy alone places the patient at unnecessary risk for a recurrent
mood episode. Although psychotherapy may be an important part of treatment, in patients with bipolar I disorder, it should be combined with
medication management.
(Choice C) This patient's bipolar I disorder is stable, and he is tolerating lithium without adverse effects; therefore, switching to an alternate
treatment (eg, valproate, quetiapine) is not indicated. Furthermore, discontinuing lithium quickly poses a high risk for relapse and even suicide.
The immediate focus should be on providing nonjudgmental education about the significant risks for medication nonadherence while encouraging
a discussion over time.
(Choice E) Given the relapse risk, an additional year of treatment followed by gradual discontinuation is contraindicated in this patient with severe
bipolar I disorder. Indefinite maintenance therapy should be recommended.
Educational objective:
Bipolar I disorder is a highly recurrent illness requiring long-term maintenance pharmacotherapy to decrease the risk for relapse. Patients asking
to stop maintenance treatment should be nonjudgmentally educated about the dangers of nonadherence.

They find that one physician orders significantly more CT scans of the head compared to other physicians in the department. The physician states
that he orders more head CT scans on young patients with chronic migraines, even those with normal examination and unremarkable history,
because he recently missed a diagnosis of intracranial bleed in an 18-year old patient with a history of chronic migraines. Which of the following
most likely explains this physician's tendency to now order excessive CT scans of the head?

Cognitive errors are unconscious biases adversely influencing clinical judgment and leading to diagnostic error. They often involve heuristics,
mental shortcuts formed based on patterns and learned associations. Heuristics represent fast, unconscious thinking (eg, impulse) rather than
measured, rational analysis; physicians who are fatigued or who work in busy clinical settings are more likely to rely on heuristics to increase
diagnostic efficiency.
This physician started ordering unnecessary head CT scans after missing a diagnosis of intracranial bleed; this behavior reflects availability
bias. Availability bias (or "recency effect") occurs when a memorable ("high-stakes"), often recent case biases subsequent judgment and
decision-making. This physician's recent experience created a mental heuristic to order head CT scans on patients with migraines. As seen in
this scenario, availability bias commonly causes excessive diagnostic workup and overtreatment.
Cognitive bias can be minimized by increasing physician awareness (eg, morbidity and mortality meetings), encouraging systematic analysis (eg,
quick-access electronic tools to calculate pre-test probability), and optimizing the environment (eg, additional staff to reduce physician burden).
(Choice B) Data misinterpretation, a cause of diagnostic error, may result from cognitive bias. For example, confirmation bias can result in
overlooking potentially concerning information on imaging or laboratory data in a patient with headache. Data misinterpretation and confirmation
bias may have triggered the physician's initial missed diagnosis in the patient with migraine. However, his tendency to subsequently order CT
scans on low-risk patients with headache reflects availability bias.
(Choice C) Documentation error involves inaccurate or incomplete record-keeping (eg, not documenting pertinent physical examination findings,
copy-and-pasting outdated information). Documentation is not a contributing factor in this scenario.
(Choice D) Knowledge deficiency (eg, insufficient ability to interpret clinical data) is a rarer cause of diagnostic error for practicing physicians
compared with cognitive error. This physician's behavior started after a recent patient experience; therefore, knowledge deficiency regarding head
CT imaging indications is unlikely.
Educational objective:
Cognitive errors involve heuristics (mental shortcuts) incorrectly influencing clinical decision-making, resulting in diagnostic error. Availability bias
describes the tendency for recent or notable clinical experiences to bias subsequent clinical judgment, and often causes excessive diagnostic
workup.

confused. The patient takes no medications and does not use tobacco or alcohol. Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is 92/50 mm Hg,

• Decreased renal perfusion

Etiology
• Displacement of intravascular fluid (eg, sepsis, pancreatitis)
• Bilateral renal artery stenosis with ACE inhibition

• Increase in serum creatinine (eg, 50% from baseline)

EABV = effective arterial blood volume; NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug.
This patient's clinical presentation (altered mental status, tachycardia, hypotension, leukocytosis, evidence of right lower lobe consolidation on
chest x-ray) is consistent with sepsis due to community-acquired pneumonia. Sepsis leads to peripheral vasodilation (hypotension) and
intravascular volume depletion (due to vascular leakage); manifestations of volume depletion in this patient include decreased appetite/poor oral
intake, dry mucous membranes, and hypernatremia. The combined effects of sepsis and volume depletion suggest that this patient has a
prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI) due to decreased renal perfusion.
Renal hypoperfusion leads to a decrease in glomerular filtration rate and a consequent increase in serum creatinine. Activation of the renin-
angiotensin-aldosterone system results in increased sodium reabsorption by the kidneys, leading to a urinary sodium of <20 mEq/L and a low
fractional excretion of sodium (<1%). Urea passively follows the reabsorption of sodium and water, resulting in an elevated blood urea
nitrogen (BUN)/creatinine ratio (≥20:1). There is no intrinsic kidney damage or infection in pure prerenal AKI; therefore, urine sediment is
bland (eg, acellular, no urinary red blood cells or white blood cells [WBCS]).
In addition to the treatment of the underlying disorder (eg, antibiotics for pneumonia), patients with prerenal Akl require volume resuscitation with
intravenous crystalloids as soon as possible to restore adequate renal perfusion.

questions.prompt:
A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following the sudden onset of excruciating left-sided chest pain. Temperature is 37.2
C (99 F), blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg, pulse is 125/min and regular, and respirations are 20/min. The patient is anxious and agitated and is
sweating profusely. Both pupils are dilated, and the nasal mucosa is atrophic. Heart sounds are regular with no murmurs or rubs. The lungs are
clear on auscultation. An initial ECG shows ST-segment depression and T-wave inversion in leads V4-V6. The first set of cardiac enzymes,
including CK-MB and troponin T, is normal. Chest x-ray reveals no acute abnormality. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in
management of this patient?
• А. Cardiac catheterization
B. Close observation
C. Intravenous diazepam
D. Intravenous metoprolol
E. Thrombolytic therapy
questions.explanation:
Clinical features of cocaine use
• Sympathetic hyperactivity: tachycardia, hypertension, dilated pupils
Clinical presentation
• Chest pain due to coronary vasoconstriction
• Psychomotor agitation, seizures
• Acute myocardial ischemia
• Aortic dissection
Complications
• ICH
• Benzodiazepines for blood pressure & anxiety
• Aspirin for inhibition of cocaine-induced platelet aggregation
Management of chest pain
• Nitroglycerin & calcium channel blockers for vasoconstrictive pain
• Immediate cardiac catheterization if indicated (eg, STEMI)
• Caution with: fibrinolysis (1 risk of ICH), beta blockers (1 risk of coronary vasoconstriction*)
*Theoretical risk due to unopposed alpha stimulation. Mixed alpha/beta blockers are sometimes considered.
ICH = intracranial hemorrhage; STEMI = ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction.
This patient has psychomotor agitation, dilated pupils, atrophic nasal mucosa, hypertension, and acute myocardial ischemia (chest pain, ECG with
ST-segment depressions and T-wave inversions), findings highly suggestive of acute cocaine intoxication. Cocaine potentiates
sympathomimetic actions by inhibiting norepinephrine reuptake into the sympathetic neuron. This stimulates alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors
and can result in coronary vasoconstriction and increases in heart rate, systemic blood pressure, and myocardial oxygen demand. It also
enhances thrombus formation by promoting platelet activation and aggregation.
All patients with acute cocaine toxicity and myocardial ischemia should be treated initially with supplemental oxygen and intravenous
benzodiazepines. By reducing sympathetic outflow, benzodiazepines (eg, diazepam) reduce anxiety and agitation, lower blood pressure and
heart rate, and alleviate cardiovascular symptoms. Aspirin slows thrombus formation; nitrates and calcium channel blockers (vasodilators) are
beneficial for cocaine-induced coronary artery vasoconstriction.
Beta blockers, including cardioselective agents (eg, metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol), generally should not be used to treat cocaine-induced
myocardial ischemia or infarction until the cocaine has been eliminated from the patient's body. Their use can theoretically cause unopposed
alpha-adrenergic stimulation and worsen coronary vasoconstriction (Choice D). Although some retrospective studies and case reports suggest
beta blocker administration is safe in patients with cocaine intoxication, methodological limitations and bias may limit the validity of their results.

alpha-adrenergic stimulation and worsen coronary vasoconstriction (Choice D). Although some retrospective studies and case reports suggest
beta blocker administration is safe in patients with cocaine intoxication, methodological limitations and bias may limit the validity of their results.
Mixed alpha and beta blockers may be safe, but the overall evidence is limited.
(Choice A) Cardiac catheterization should be performed in patients with STEMI and in those with persistent chest pain despite aggressive
optimal medical therapy.
(Choice B) This patient has signs of acute cocaine toxicity and ongoing myocardial ischemia. Observation is not appropriate.
(Choice E) Thrombolytic agents are indicated only in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) when timely access to
coronary angiography is not available. Their use has been associated with increased rates of intracranial hemorrhage in patients with cocaine
use. A small number of patients with cocaine-associated chest pain can also have aortic dissection, which was not ruled out in this patient.
Administering a thrombolytic agent in that setting could be catastrophic and is absolutely contraindicated.
Educational objective:
Patients with cocaine-associated chest pain should be treated initially with intravenous benzodiazepines. These improve the symptoms of
psychomotor agitation, reduce myocardial oxygen demand, and alleviate cardiovascular symptoms. Aspirin, nitroglycerin, and calcium channel
blockers are also effective in the initial management of cocaine-associated chest pain. Beta blockers are generally not recommended.

questions.prompt:
An 18-year-old student is brought to the emergency department due to dizziness and weakness. The patient was studying for final exams with her
friends when she suddenly felt dizzy and started having palpitations. She tried to get up but felt weak and had to sit back down. The patient has
had several similar episodes in the past 2 months. She lives with her parents and commutes to a nearby college. She has no prior medical
conditions. Family history includes diabetes mellitus in her father. The patient reports occasional alcohol use. Temperature is 37 C (98.6 F),
blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 16/min. There are no orthostatic changes. BMI is 19 kg/m2. Physical
examination shows no abnormalities. Finger-stick glucose is 48 mg/dL. Symptoms promptly resolve with intravenous dextrose. Serum insulin
and C-peptide levels, drawn prior to dextrose administration, are elevated. Which of the following best explains this patient's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Factitious disorder (imposed on self)
• Intentional falsification of illness:
• Feigning illness
Behavioral
• Self-induced illness
characteristics
• Exacerbation of preexisting illness
• Motivation by internal factors rather than external gain (eg, financial compensation)
• Overt/dramatic symptoms
Clinical
• Frequent visits for medical care
presentation
• Patient possibly refusing consent to release records or tampering with test samples
• More common in health care workers
• Direct observation or discovery of medical supplies (eg, medications, syringes)
Diagnostic
• Confirmatory testing (eg, sulfonylurea screen, stool laxative screen)
confirmation
• Medical record review
This patient has symptomatic hypoglycemia, and the elevated insulin and C-peptide levels suggest that this is due to excessive endogenous
secretion of insulin because C-peptide is cosecreted with endogenous insulin but not present in injectable insulins. Although this could be due
to an autonomous insulin-secreting islet cell tumor (ie, insulinoma), such tumors are very rare and usually occur at age >40. Surreptitious use of
a sulfonylurea or other insulin secretagogue is much more likely, particularly in a patient with a family member who has diabetes mellitus or other
access to prescription medications (eg, pharmacy worker). The diagnosis can be confirmed with a hypoglycemic drug screen.
Factitious disorder is characterized by intentional falsification of illness in the absence of external reward (eg, financial compensation,
disability benefits). Patients with factitious disorder appear to be motivated by internal factors, such as psychosocial stressors (eg, college
workload, final examinations) or desire for validation. A history of major childhood illness or abuse is associated with increased risk, but the
etiology is poorly understood. Treatment primarily includes psychotherapy.
(Choice A) Binge alcohol drinking can cause hypoglycemia due to depletion of hepatic glycogen, impaired gluconeogenesis, and altered
counterregulatory hormone (eg, epinephrine) secretion. However, this patient's elevated insulin and C-peptide levels indicate excessive
endogenous insulin secretion as the cause.
(Choice B) Patients with factitious disorder may induce hypoglycemia by injecting exogenous insulin. However, exogenous insulin preparations
do not contain C-peptide, so levels would be low.
(Choices C and D) Phentermine is a centrally acting appetite suppressant that can cause short-term weight loss in patients with obesity.
However, reduced caloric intake, whether due to anorexiants or simple dietary restriction, rarely causes severe hypoglycemia because of the
induction of multiple counterregulatory factors (ie, glucagon, cortisol, epinephrine, growth hormone). In addition, C-peptide would not be elevated.
(Choice E) Self-induced vomiting (eg, due to an eating disorder) can cause dizziness and weakness due to the resulting metabolic derangements
(eg, hypovolemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypochloremia) but would not cause increased endogenous insulin secretion. Patients would often have
orthostatic hypotension.
Educational objective:
Factitious disorder is characterized by intentional falsification of illness in the absence of external reward. Patients appear to be motivated by
internal factors, such as psychosocial stressors or desire for validation. Patients with factitious disorder may have hypoglycemia due to the
surreptitious intake of sulfonylureas or insulin.

implantation), and a negative progesterone withdrawal test (despite normal estrogen and progesterone levels). Some patients may have cyclic
pelvic pain if the endometrial cavity is not totally obliterated due to small pockets of obstructed, proliferative endometrium. A hysteroscopy is
performed for diagnosis and treatment via lysis of adhesions.
(Choice A) Endometriosis causes cyclic pelvic pain (ie, dysmenorrhea) due to ectopic endometrial implants, which trigger intraabdominal
inflammation, scarring, and distortion of pelvic architecture, resulting in a fixed, tender uterus. Although endometriosis causes infertility, it is not
associated with amenorrhea.
(Choice C) Uterine fibroids may recur and cause pelvic pain secondary to uterine enlargement and a mass effect on the bowel and bladder. In
addition, intracavitary and submucosal fibroids are associated with infertility and recurrent spontaneous abortion. Although this patient has had
fibroids, a recurrent fibroid would cause regular, heavy menses rather than amenorrhea, making this diagnosis unlikely.
(Choice D) Tubal occlusion may occur due to adhesions from pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, or prior pelvic surgery. Although tubal
blockage is a common cause of infertility, this patient has none of these risk factors.
(Choice E) A uterine septum is a uterine lateral fusion defect resulting in 2 uterine cavities. Due to the small and poorly vascularized uterine
cavities, patients with a septate uterus are at increased risk of recurrent spontaneous abortion, fetal growth restriction, and preterm delivery. A
uterine septum does not cause amenorrhea or infertility.
Educational objective:
Intrauterine synechiae (ie, Asherman syndrome) is a complication of intrauterine surgeries such as hysteroscopic myomectomy or curettage. Due
to the scarring of the endometrial cavity, patients often have amenorrhea, infertility, and a negative progesterone withdrawal test.

A 62-year-old woman who works as a high school administrative assistant is brought to the emergency department by her coworker. She states
that 2 hours ago she suddenly felt dizzy while sitting at her desk. A short time later, the patient tried to stand to go to the bathroom and felt like

scan of the head is normal. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?

Because she is being seen within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, thrombolysis with intravenous alteplase is the best next step in management.

questions.prompt:
A 38-year-old woman at 6 weeks gestation comes to the office due to vaginal bleeding. The patient has had intermittent bleeding for the past
week, which increases after intercourse. She has had no pelvic pain, nausea, or vomiting. Blood pressure is 124/68 mm Hg and pulse is 86/min.
The abdomen is soft and nontender, without rebound or guarding. On pelvic examination, there is dark brown discharge pooling in the posterior
vaginal vault. The cervix is closed, and there is a raised cervical mass that bleeds freely when manipulated with a swab. Ultrasound reveals a
yolk sac and a 6-week intrauterine fetal pole with cardiac motion. Blood type is O, Rh positive. Which of the following is the best next step in
management of this patient?

Carcinoma in situ

Advanced stage

This patient's irregular vaginal bleeding and cervical mass are classic for invasive cervical cancer, which typically presents in patients who have
not had routine Pap test screening. Other risk factors include immunosuppression, tobacco use, and multiple sexual partners.
Although cervical cancer can be asymptomatic, patients typically have vaginal bleeding, particularly after intercourse (eg, postcoital) due to
trauma to the cervix. Pregnancy, which increases pelvic vascularity, may increase the risk of bleeding from a cervical mass. On examination,
Cuvona
This patient's irregular vaginal bleeding and cervical mass are classic for invasive cervical cancer, which typically presents in patients who have
not had routine Pap test screening. Other risk factors include immunosuppression, tobacco use, and multiple sexual partners.
Although cervical cancer can be asymptomatic, patients typically have vaginal bleeding, particularly after intercourse (eg, postcoital) due to
trauma to the cervix. Pregnancy, which increases pelvic vascularity, may increase the risk of bleeding from a cervical mass. On examination,
patients typically have cervical friability (eg, bleeding with manipulation) and a raised, exophytic mass, as seen in this patient. Other features
may include ulcerative lesions (due to tissue necrosis) and watery, mucoid vaginal discharge.
Cervical lesions suspicious for cancer require cervical biopsy, which can be performed safely during pregnancy. Patients with cervical cancer
who are pregnant (such as this patient) require specialized oncology and obstetric management, and any diagnostic delay can increase the risk of
cancer progression.
(Choice A) Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are empiric treatment for acute cervicitis, which can present with postcoital bleeding. However,
cervicitis typically causes mucopurulent discharge, a finding not seen in this patient, and is not associated with a cervical mass.
(Choice C) Endometrial biopsy may be indicated in certain patients with abnormal uterine, not cervical, bleeding to exclude endometrial cancer.
However, it is not performed in pregnancy due to the risk of pregnancy loss. Given her friable cervical mass with intermittent/postcoital vaginal
bleeding consistent with cervical cancer, this patient should undergo cervical biopsy.
(Choice D) Expectant management is indicated for first-trimester bleeding due to threatened abortion (eg, vaginal bleeding). Although this patient
has a viable intrauterine pregnancy (eg, yolk sac, intrauterine fetal pole with cardiac motion), her cervical lesion requires further evaluation.
(Choice E) Kleihauer-Betke testing is required in Rh-negative patients with heavy vaginal bleeding during pregnancy to evaluate for fetomaternal
hemorrhage that can lead to Rh-alloimmunization; prevention is with anti-D immunoglobulin (ie, RhoGAM). This patient is Rh-positive.
(Choice F) Quantitative B-hCG levels are measured to evaluate for ectopic pregnancy. Once an intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac motion is
identified, B-hCG levels do not change management and therefore are not measured.
Educational objective:
Cervical cancer typically presents with irregular vaginal bleeding (eg, postcoital) and a friable, exophytic cervical mass. Suspicious cervical
lesions require biopsy, which is typically safe during pregnancy.

Clinical features of anabolic steroid abuse
Musculoskeletal
• 1 Muscle mass
• Low testosterone, FSH, LH
• Testicular atrophy
Reproductive
• Spermatogenesis
• Normal libido & erectile function (during use)
• J Libido, impotence (during withdrawal)
Endocrine

Hematologic
• Erythrocytosis
• Affective symptoms
Psychological

• Acne
Dermatologic/breast
• Gynecomastia
This patient's increased aggression, accelerated male pattern baldness, and gynecomastia are concerning for anabolic (androgenic) steroid
use. Anabolic steroids are popular among people who want to improve their physical appearance and athletic performance (eg, build muscle,
increase strength). Some of the agents used for these purposes are testosterone, trenbolone, boldenone, stanozolol, and nandrolone.
Anabolic steroid adverse effects include impaired endogenous testicular function and decreased testicular size and sperm count, resulting in
male-factor infertility. Liver dysfunction may occur, and patients can develop erythrocytosis due to androgen-stimulated erythropoiesis. HDL
levels decrease, and high doses may even cause cardiac dysfunction. Gynecomastia can develop when excess testosterone is converted to
estradiol, leading to breast enlargement. Skin changes include acne and premature or accelerated male pattern baldness. Psychiatric effects
include aggression and mood disturbances that are often complicated by concurrent alcohol use.
(Choice A) Growth hormone may be taken to improve athletic performance. It can lead to hyperglycemia, sodium retention, and hypertension.
Patients may also have swollen hands and joint and muscle pain, which are not reported in this case.
(Choice B) Methamphetamine is a CNS stimulant associated with complications such as hypertension, tachycardia, severe agitation or
aggressiveness, and psychosis. Patients may have acne or facial sores due to skin picking, as well as male pattern baldness. However,
gynecomastia is absent.
(Choice C) Phencyclidine (PCP) causes brief dissociative psychotic episodes. Patients taking PCP may be aggressive and less sensitive to pain
but do not develop acne, baldness, or gynecomastia.
(Choice D) Tamoxifen, a nonsteroidal anti-estrogen agent, competes with estrogen at estrogen receptors in the breast and is taken by anabolic
steroid users to treat gynecomastia.
(Choice F) Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) may cause increased appetite, red eyes, slowed reflexes, dizziness, and impaired coordination. THC
use may lead to gynecomastia but is unlikely to cause aggression.
Educational objective:
Anabolic-androgenic steroids are used to improve physique and athletic performance but are associated with numerous adverse effects, including
acne, baldness, gynecomastia, liver dysfunction, altered lipid profiles, virilization, testicular failure, and possible mood and behavior changes.

BSA = body surface area; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs;
SJS = Stevens-Johnson syndrome; TEN = toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) represents a serious inflammatory reaction to certain drugs (eg,
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) or infections (eg, Mycoplasma pneumoniae). Clinical features include coalescing erythematous macules,
bullae, desquamation, and mucositis. Systemic signs are common and may include fever, tachycardia, hypotension, altered level of
consciousness, seizures, and coma. By convention, SJS denotes <10% of body surface area involvement, >30% is designated as toxic epidermal
necrolysis (TEN), and 10%-30% is SJS/TEN overlap.
The diagnosis is based on the typical mucocutaneous lesions, systemic signs, and exposure to a likely causative medication. Treatment is
supportive, with aggressive fluid support and wound care similar to that for burns. Secondary infections are common, and fatalities may occur
desnite treatment
• Graft versus host disease
BSA = body surface area; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs;
SJS = Stevens-Johnson syndrome; TEN = toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN) represents a serious inflammatory reaction to certain drugs (eg,
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) or infections (eg, Mycoplasma pneumoniae). Clinical features include coalescing erythematous macules,
bullae, desquamation, and mucositis. Systemic signs are common and may include fever, tachycardia, hypotension, altered level of
consciousness, seizures, and coma. By convention, SJS denotes <10% of body surface area involvement, >30% is designated as toxic epidermal
necrolysis (TEN), and 10%-30% is SJS/TEN overlap.
The diagnosis is based on the typical mucocutaneous lesions, systemic signs, and exposure to a likely causative medication. Treatment is
supportive, with aggressive fluid support and wound care similar to that for burns. Secondary infections are common, and fatalities may occur
despite treatment.
(Choice B) Impetigo is a staphylococcal or streptococcal skin infection characterized by red macules and papular lesions with honey-colored
crusts. It is most common in children.
(Choice C) Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by autoantibodies to desmosomes. Like SJS/TEN, it can cause mucosal lesions and desquamating
bullae. However, systemic signs (eg, fever) are less prominent, and the course is typically more chronic, with oral lesions appearing weeks to
months prior to skin symptoms.
(Choice D) Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is usually seen in children age <6. It is a syndrome of acute exfoliation caused by toxins
produced by Staphylococcus aureus.
(Choice F) Toxic shock syndrome is an inflammatory response caused by a staphylococcal exotoxin and presents with fever, rash, hypotension,
constitutional symptoms, and multiorgan injury. The rash is characterized by diffuse erythema resembling sunburn, with desquamation involving
the palms and soles.
Educational objective:
Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis represents an inflammatory reaction to drugs or certain infections and is characterized by
coalescing erythematous macules, bullae, desquamation, and mucositis. Systemic signs include fever, hemodynamic instability, and altered level
of consciousness.

A 62-year-old woman is sent to the emergency department from her rehabilitation facility due to sudden-onset dyspnea and nonproductive cough.
The symptoms started acutely while the patient was trying to get out of bed. She has no subjective fever, hemoptysis, wheezing, palpitations, leg
pain, or lower-extremity edema. The patient underwent right knee replacement 2 weeks ago for severe degenerative joint disease. Her other
medical problems include peptic ulcer disease from nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory use, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She drinks
alcohol socially and does not use tobacco. Her temperature is 38 C (100.4 F), blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations
are 22/min. Pulse oximetry is 91% on room air. BMI is 36 kg/m2. The patient is alert and cooperative without cyanosis or jaundice. Lungs are
clear to auscultation. The abdomen is soft, nondistended, and nontender. Right knee is without erythema, warmth, or tenderness. ECG shows
sinus tachycardia. Chest x-ray is normal. Complete blood count shows a leukocyte count of 6,500/mm'. Which of the following is the best next
step in management of this patient?

This patient's dramatic postoperative presentation with sudden-onset dyspnea, nonproductive cough, tachycardia, and mild hypoxia is highly
suggestive of acute pulmonary embolism (PE). Early, effective anticoagulation decreases the mortality risk of acute PE and should be
considered in patients without absolute contraindications (eg, hemorrhagic stroke, massive gastrointestinal bleed).
Peptic ulcer disease is not an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation, although it increases risk of bleeding with anticoagulation. This
patient's modified Wells score is 6 (absence of a more likely diagnosis = 3 points, tachycardia = 1.5 points, immobilization due to recent knee
surgery = 1.5 points), which correlates to PE being likely (modified Wells score >4). Given that she is clinically stable (normotensive, mild
hypoxemia) with no evidence of distress, the diagnosis of PE can be confirmed with CT angiography (CTA). If CTA confirms PE, clinical judgment
can dictate whether anticoagulation is initiated or other options are pursued (eg, inferior vena cava filter placement) based on the estimated risk of
bleeding from the peptic ulcer.
(Choice A) Rapid collection of blood cultures and initiation of antibiotics are appropriate when sepsis is suspected. This patient has a normal
leukocyte count, clear lungs, a normal-appearing right knee, and no other evidence of localizing infection. Her tachycardia and low-grade fever
can be explained by PE, which is the most likely diagnosis and essential to rule out.
(Choice C) D-dimer testing can be helpful in patients presenting with unlikely probability of PE (modified Wells score ≤4). However, a negative
test result cannot be used to reliably exclude PE in patients with a modified Wells score >4.
(Choice D) Compression ultrasonography is the preferred initial test for diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis (DVT). This patient has no clinical
manifestations of DVT. In addition, a negative ultrasound result does not rule out PE.
(Choice E) Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) may show acute PE findings of increased right ventricular size and right ventricular
dysfunction. However, these findings are often only seen in massive PE accompanied by syncope, shock, and hemodynamic instability.
Therefore, TTE is generally reserved for clinically decompensating patients in whom CTA cannot be obtained.
Educational objective:
The modified Wells criteria can assess the pretest possibility of acute pulmonary embolism (PE). CT angiography is the test of choice in clinically
stable patients in whom PE is likely. Empiric anticoagulation in these patients is often appropriate, but clinical judgment is needed regarding
clinical stability and contraindications.

Obesity and cardiovascular disease are common comorbidities in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. This patient has suboptimal glycemic
control on metformin (a first-line diabetic treatment) and requires additional therapy; he should ideally be given an add-on diabetic agent that
reduces cardiovascular mortality, induces weight loss, and carries a low risk for hypoglycemia (which increases coronary ischemia-related
mortality). Suitable agents include glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and certain sodium-glucose cotransporter-2
(SGLT-2) inhibitors:
• GLP-1RAs (eg, exenatide, liraglutide) regulate glucose by increasing glucose-dependent insulin release (ie, low risk for hypoglycemia)
and suppressing glucagon. They also slow gastric emptying, which decreases appetite and causes weight loss.
• SGLT-2 inhibitors (eg, canagliflozin, empagliflozin) increase renal glucose and sodium excretion, leading to mild weight loss and mild
diuresis. Because renal glucose filtration is proportional to serum glucose level, hypoglycemia is rare. These agents also reduce heart
failure-related mortality and progression of diabetic nephropathy.
(Choice A) Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (eg, sitagliptin) prevent degradation of GLP-1 and therefore function like GLP-1RAs. However, they
are less potent than GLP-1RAs and are not associated with weight loss or cardioprotective effects.

and risk for hypoglycemia. Compared to GLP-1RAs or SGLT2 inhibitors, these agents are less preferred for patients with obesity and coronary

questions.prompt:
A 65-year-old, right-handed man comes to the emergency department due to sudden-onset, right-sided weakness. The patient was watching
television an hour ago, when his family noted that his face appeared "twisted." He also experienced weakness of his right arm and leg but no
headache, nausea, vomiting, or loss of consciousness. The patient has a history of hypertension and is nonadherent with medications. He is a
former smoker with a 20-pack-year history. Temperature is 36.7 C (98.1 F), blood pressure is 164/72 mm Hg, pulse is 65/min, and respirations are
14/min. Physical examination shows weakness of the right lower face and right upper and lower extremities. Pupillary reflexes, ocular
movements, and visual field testing are normal bilaterally. Speech is without aphasia, and the patient correctly names his left and right arms.
Sensory examination is normal throughout. Noncontrast CT scan of the head reveals no intracranial bleeding. Which of the following is the most
likely site of a lesion in this patient?

This patient has had a stroke, resulting in hemiparesis of the right arm, leg, and lower face. Strokes in many locations in the CNS can result in
hemiparesis (which is nearly always contralateral to the site of ischemia) and can often be further localized by their associated features.
• Cerebral cortex: Cortical signs (ie, deficits that specifically localize to the cortex) that may include Visual disturbances (eg, hemianopia,
gaze preference), Aphasia (ie, typically expressive Broca), Neglect, and cortical Sensory deficits (eg, inability to recognize movement drawn
on the palm). It is evaluated with the VAN(S) stroke scale.
• Internal capsule: Often pure motor. Cranial nerves are not involved except the upper motor neuron-type (UMN-type) facial nerve; sensory
deficits are uncommon.
• Brainstem: Ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits. Cranial nerves impacted can further localize to the midbrain (CN III, IV), pons (CN VI, VII
[lower motor neuron pattern], VIII), and medulla (CN IX-XII).
This patient has right hemiparesis with an UMN pattern of facial weakness (ie, weakness of lower face with sparing of forehead). He has no
cortical signs or sensory deficits, so cortical stroke is unlikely; he has no cranial nerve deficits other than the facial nerve (UMN type), so brainstem
stroke is unlikely. The hemiparesis is likely due to a stroke affecting the left internal capsule, supplied by the deep penetrating, lenticulostriate
arteries. This is also known as a lacunar stroke.
(Choice A) A stroke in the left frontoparietal cortex could lead to right hemiparesis, but a cortical stroke large enough to result in face, arm, and
leg weakness would also likely result in sensory disturbances and cortical signs such as visual disturbances, aphasia, and/or neglect.
(Choices C and F) A lesion in the pons would likely be accompanied by pontine ipsilateral (ie, crossed signs) cranial nerve palsies (CN VI-VIII).
(Choice D) A stroke impacting the right frontoparietal cortex would lead to left hemiparesis and cortical signs (eg, neglect, visual changes,
sensory changes, aphasia [dominant hemisphere]).
(Choice E) A stroke impacting the right internal capsule could lead to a pure motor stroke, as seen in this patient, but hemiparesis would be
contralateral to the lesion, resulting in left hemiparesis rather than right.
Educational objective:
A stroke causing hemiparesis can usually be further localized based on the associated symptoms. A pure motor stroke with no cortical signs or
cranial nerve deficits is likely due to a lesion in the contralateral internal capsule.
