questions.prompt:
A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 29 weeks gestation comes to the emergency department due to right-sided abdominal pain. The pain
developed yesterday morning, initially resolved with acetaminophen, but has become increasingly severe over the past few hours. The patient
now has continuous nausea and has vomited twice. She has not had a bowel movement in 2 days. She has had uterine contractions, but no
vaginal bleeding or leakage of fluid. The patient has no chronic medical conditions, and her only surgery was a cesarean delivery for failure to
progress. Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 118/min. BMI is 30 kg/m?. Fetal heart rate monitoring
shows a baseline of 160/min and no decelerations. Tocodynamometry shows regular uterine contractions every 1-2 minutes. The abdomen is
tender to palpation, but has no rebound or guarding. The uterus has fundal tenderness and an associated firm, tender mass. On pelvic
examination, the cervix is closed. Leukocyte count is 19,000/mm'. Urinalysis is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this
patient?
questions.explanation:
This patient at 29 weeks gestation has acute-onset, right-sided abdominal pain. Abdominal pain in pregnancy can have a variety of etiologies
from both benign and life-threatening causes. This patient with fundal tenderness and a firm, tender mass most likely has a degenerating uterine
leiomyoma.
Leiomyomata uteri (fibroids) are benign myometrial tumors that can grow rapidly during pregnancy due to elevated estrogen and progesterone
levels. However, because myometrial blood flow shifts toward the developing fetus and placenta during pregnancy, fibroids can outgrow their
blood supply, leading to fibroid infarction and necrosis. Therefore, degenerating fibroids cause uterine contractions (due to prostaglandin
release) and fundal tenderness, a tender mass, and leukocytosis (due to inflammatory cytokine release), as seen in this patient.
Diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasound, and the condition is conservatively managed with acute pain control (eg, indomethacin for patients <32
weeks gestation).
(Choice A) Pregnant women are more likely to develop cholelithiasis and acute cholecystitis due to elevated estrogen levels. Patients can have
right-sided abdominal pain, vomiting, and leukocytosis; however, acute cholecystitis is unlikely to cause a firm, tender mass with fundal
tenderness, making this diagnosis less likely.
(Choice B) Acute diverticulitis can cause abdominal pain and leukocytosis; however, patients typically have pain in the left lower, rather than the
right upper, quadrant due to sigmoid colon involvement. In addition, this patient has fundal tenderness with an associated firm mass, making
acute diverticulitis less likely.
(Choice C) Acute pyelonephritis can cause preterm contractions and leukocytosis. In contrast to this patient with fibroid degeneration, those with
pyelonephritis have flank pain, no associated abdominal mass, and an abnormal urinalysis (eg, nitrites, leukocyte esterase).
(Choice E) Uterine rupture, which can occur in patients with prior cesarean delivery, can present with acute abdominal pain and a palpable mass
(ie, fetal parts). However, patients typically have fetal heart rate decelerations and an acute abdomen (eg, rebound, guarding), findings not seen
in this patient.
Educational objective:
Leiomyomata uteri are more likely to degenerate during pregnancy because myometrial blood flow shifts toward the developing fetus and
placenta. An infarcted, degenerating uterine fibroid can cause severe abdominal pain; uterine tenderness; a palpable, firm, and tender mass; and
signs of inflammation (eg, leukocytosis).

home, and this is his first medical evaluation. He is breastfed exclusively. Vital signs are within normal limits. Several ecchymoses are visible on
the extremities. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory results are as follows:
Platelets
270,000/mm3

26 sec

42 sec

18 sec (normal: 15-20)

questions.explanation:
Infantile vitamin K-deficient bleeding
• Low vitamin K stores (poor placental transfer, sterile gut, low content in breast milk)
Pathophysiology
• Inefficient vitamin K use by immature liver
• Classically presents on day 2-7 of life*
• Easy bruising
Clinical features
• Umbilical, mucosal & gastrointestinal bleeding
• Intracranial hemorrhage
• 1 PT
Laboratory findings
• 1 PTT (if severe)
• Normal platelet count
Prevention
• Intramuscular vitamin K at birth
*Can occur up to age 6 months.
This neonate who has not received prior medical care has bruising and prolonged PT and PTT, findings concerning for vitamin K-deficient
bleeding (VKDB).
Vitamin K is essential for enzymatic carboxylation and activation of coagulation factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X. Newborns are vitamin K
deficient due to poor placental transfer, lack of intestinal flora to synthesize vitamin K, and immature liver function (ie, poor vitamin K utilization).
Therefore, intramuscular vitamin K is given at birth to prevent spontaneous bleeding. Neonates who do not receive this injection, such as
this patient, are at highest risk of VKDB, particularly if exclusively breastfed because breast milk contains insufficient vitamin K.
Classic VKDB presents on day 2-7 of life with easy bruising, mucosal bleeding (eg, epistaxis), gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and/or
intracranial hemorrhage. Late-onset disease can occur up to age 6 months. Because of reduced coagulation factor carboxylation, laboratory
evaluation shows prolonged PT and, in severe deficiency, prolonged PTT. The diagnosis is confirmed by the reversal of laboratory
abnormalities with vitamin K administration.
(Choice A) Afibrinogenemia is a rare, autosomal recessive bleeding disorder characterized by absent fibrinogen production. Severe bleeding
classically develops at the site of the umbilical cord after birth. Like PT and PTT, thrombin time is prolonged.
(Choice B) Disseminated intravascular coagulation typically presents with bleeding (eg, bruising, intravenous site oozing) due to consumption of
platelets and clotting factors. Laboratory findings include prolonged PT and PTT and thrombocytopenia. This patient's platelet count is normal.

platelets and clotting factors. Laboratory findings include prolonged PT and PTT and thrombocytopenia. This patient's platelet count is normal.
(Choices C and D) Severe von Willebrand disease (characterized by impaired synthesis of von Willebrand factor) and factor VIll deficiency
(hemophilia A) can present with easy bruising and bleeding in the neonatal period. Both conditions have a prolonged PTT but normal PT.
(Choice E) Impaired platelet function can be caused by medications (eg, aspirin), metabolic conditions (eg, uremia, liver disease), or congenital
disorders (eg, Glanzmann thrombasthenia). Patients have mucocutaneous bleeding and petechiae; PT, PTT, and platelet count are normal.
Educational objective:
Vitamin K-deficient bleeding classically presents with bleeding in newborns (day 2-7 of life) who did not receive intramuscular vitamin K, which is
essential in the enzymatic carboxylation and activation of coagulation factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X. Symptoms include easy bruising,
mucosal bleeding, gastrointestinal bleeding, and/or intracranial hemorrhage; laboratory evaluation reveals prolonged PT with or without prolonged
PTT.

questions.prompt:
A 32-year-old woman comes to the office due to feeling down for the past several months. The patient has had persistent tiredness, lack of
motivation, memory impairment, and loss of libido. She also has had anorexia but reports an unusual craving for foods like salty pretzels or potato
chips. Menses occur at regular intervals. The patient does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs and works as a fashion designer. Blood
pressure is 110/62 mm Hg and pulse is 88/min. BMI is 19.8 kg/m2 with weight of 54 kg (119 lb), which is 15 kg (33 lb) lower than her previous
weight. The lungs are clear on auscultation and heart sounds are normal. The abdomen is soft and nontender with no organomegaly. There is
decreased axillary and pubic hair. Mental status examination reveals a restricted affect. She has no suicidal ideation. Which of the following is
most likely to establish the diagnosis in this patient?

options.label: CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis

questions.explanation:
In the evaluation of depression, medical causes of depressed mood should always be considered. Although this patient's fatigue, anorexia,
memory impairment, lack of motivation, and loss of libido can be attributed to major depressive disorder (MDD), salt craving and reduced body
hair are suggestive of primary adrenal insufficiency (PAI) (also known as Addison disease). PAl usually results from autoimmune destruction of
the bilateral adrenal cortex and presents with the following:
• Mineralocorticoid deficiency causes renal salt wasting, with hypotension, weight loss, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and dietary salt
craving.
• Glucocorticoid deficiency leads to fatigue, anorexia, and many psychiatric manifestations of adrenal insufficiency (eg, irritability,
depressed mood). It also contributes to hypotension.
• Androgen deficiency leads to loss of libido and suppression of secondary sexual characteristics (eg, reduced pubic hair). These effects
are typically only seen in women because androgen production still occurs in the testes of men.
In patients with suspected Al, salt craving and hyperpigmentation are specific for PAI and help differentiate it from secondary Al. The diagnosis of
PAl is made by stimulation testing with cosyntropin, a synthetic form of ACTH. Low production of cortisol following cosyntropin administration
is diagnostic of PAI.
(Choice B) CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis can help identify malignancy. Small cell lung cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma can rarely
cause paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis, which manifests with mood changes and memory loss. However, this would not account for dietary salt
craving and reduced secondary sexual characteristics.
(Choice C) A detailed nutritional history may help diagnose anorexia nervosa, which is commonly associated with MDD. However, anorexia
nervosa usually requires BMI <18.5 kg/m2 and is commonly accompanied by amenorrhea; in addition, salt craving makes PAI more likely.
(Choice D) Acute HIV infection can present with fatigue and weight loss; however, hepatomegaly and/or splenomegaly is often present as well.
In addition, it would not explain salt craving and reduced secondary sexual characteristics.
(Choice E) Symptomatic improvement with antidepressant therapy may help confirm suspected MDD; however, this patient's symptoms are more
consistent with depressed mood secondary to an underlying medical condition. Once a diagnosis of PAI is confirmed, treatment with
corticosteroid replacement therapy is most appropriate.
Educational objective:
In patients with depressed mood, an underlying medical condition should be considered and may be suggested by findings that are unexplained
by psychiatric illness alone. Primary adrenal insufficiency presents with clinical manifestations of deficiency of mineralocorticoids (eg, dietary salt
craving), glucocorticoids (eg, fatigue, depressed mood), and androgens (eg, reduced secondary sexual characteristics in women).

questions.prompt:
A 38-year-old woman comes to the office for follow-up of major depressive disorder. She was first seen 2 weeks ago for low mood and irritability,
loss of interest, difficulty falling and staying asleep, decreased appetite, and poor concentration at work. At that time, she was started on a
therapeutic dosage of escitalopram and weekly psychotherapy. The patient had mild nausea for several days after starting the medication but is
now tolerating it without difficulty. She says, "I'm afraid the medication isn't working as well anymore. At first my sleep and appetite were better,
but for the past few days I feel like I might be slipping back to where I started." The patient reports that she is stressed because her husband is
away on business this week and her father was recently hospitalized for a stroke. Mental status examination shows a mildly depressed mood and
sad affect. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer
() 04 secs
Time Spent
F
Explanation
Assessment of antidepressant medication response requires that the patient has had an adequate trial in both dose and duration. An adequate
antidepressant trial is generally considered to be at least 4-6 weeks at a therapeutic dosage. This patient has taken escitalopram for only 2
weeks, which is considered an inadequate trial in duration. Her lack of sustained improvement after 2 weeks is not uncommon, and her symptoms
over the past week are likely related in part to psychosocial stress (father hospitalized, husband away).
The most appropriate step in pharmacotherapy is to continue the trial of escitalopram at the current dosage. Increasing the dosage is
unnecessary and risks exposing the patient to additional side effects (Choice E). The patient should be educated that 2 weeks is considered an
inadequate trial and encouraged to continue the medication for at least 2-4 more weeks. Patients should receive an adequate antidepressant trial
before next-step treatments are recommended, such as augmentation with a second medication or switching to an alternate antidepressant.
(Choices A and B) It would be premature to add amitriptyline at bedtime or aripiprazole after only 2 weeks of escitalopram. These augmentation
strategies could be considered in a patient who has failed an adequate trial of monotherapy.
(Choices C and D) Discontinuing antidepressant medication at the 2-week point would be premature. Switching to an alternate antidepressant
can be considered for patients with minimal response after an adequate trial of 4-6 weeks or for those unable to tolerate the medication.
Trazodone is a very sedating medication that is often difficult to tolerate in dosages required to treat depression.
Educational objective:
An antidepressant trial is at least 4-6 weeks at a therapeutic dose. Physicians should continue antidepressants for at least 4-6 weeks before
considering the next step in treatment.

Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
• Gastric suction or severe vomiting
Common etiologies
• Loop or thiazide diuretic overuse
• Gastric or renal H+ losses initiate alkalosis
• Volume depletion activates RAAS
Pathophysiology
• 1 Renal K* & H* losses cause hypokalemia & worsen alkalosis
• Relatively greater loss of CI than Na* → profound CI depletion
• J CI impairs renal HCO3 excretion to perpetuate alkalosis
• Remove or treat initiating factor
Management
• CI replenishment with normal saline corrects alkalosis
RAAS = renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
This patient has had severe vomiting (possibly due to an untreated peptic ulcer) and now has evidence of volume depletion (eg, dry mucous
membranes, tachycardia). Vomiting causes a significant loss of gastric H* from the body. It also causes loss of water and salt (NaCI), with
relatively more loss of Cl- than Na* due to the high gastric quantity of hydrochloric acid (HCI). These losses trigger characteristic electrolyte
abnormalities resulting in hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
• The loss of H* reduces the amount of carbonic acid (H2CO3) buffer in the body, resulting in an increase in the relative quantity of bicarbonate
(HCO3). Metabolic alkalosis is initiated with increased serum HCO3:
• Volume loss decreases renal perfusion and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. The secondary hyperaldosteronism
stimulates Na* reabsorption in the distal tubules at the expense of increased K* and H* excretion. This leads to hypokalemia and worsens
the metabolic alkalosis.
• The loss of Cl from the stomach and kidneys (which is relatively greater than the passive Cl reabsorption that aldosterone stimulates along
with Na* reabsorption) leads to profound total body Cl depletion and hypochloremia. Because adequate Cl delivery to the distal renal
tubules is required for appropriate excretion of HCO3 (via the pendrin exchanger), the Cl depletion causes impaired HCO, excretion and
perpetuates the metabolic alkalosis.

chloride is an important indicator of the etiology and appropriate treatment of metabolic alkalosis. It is the expected finding in etiologies of

This child with multiple episodes of simple cystitis (ie, no fever, flank pain) over the past year has recurrent cystitis. There are a variety of risk
factors for recurrent cystitis in children; in this patient, this is most likely secondary to her functional constipation. Young children are at risk for
functional constipation during times of dietary changes that alter stool consistency (eg, introduction of cow's milk and solid foods) or during the
onset of stressors that cause withholding behavior (eg, toilet training, starting school/day care).
In patients who develop chronic constipation, the retained feces cause the rectum to progressively dilate. The hard stool in the dilated rectum
distorts and compresses the bladder and urethra, which prevents complete voiding and leads to urinary retention and stasis in the bladder.
As a result, the residual urine becomes a potential breeding ground for bacteria that ascend through the urethra from the perineum, causing
cystitis.
Therefore, in addition to treating the recurrent cystitis, additional management includes treatment of the underlying risk factor. In patients with
tunctional constipation, this involves long-term laxative therapy to sotten stools, prevent stool withholding, and allow the rectum to return to normal
size, thereby relieving the pressure on the bladder.

As a result, the residual urine becomes a potential breeding ground for bacteria that ascend through the urethra from the perineum, causing
cystitis.
Therefore, in addition to treating the recurrent cystitis, additional management includes treatment of the underlying risk factor. In patients with
functional constipation, this involves long-term laxative therapy to soften stools, prevent stool withholding, and allow the rectum to return to normal
size, thereby relieving the pressure on the bladder.
(Choice A) Inadequate treatment of a prior infection is unlikely due to the 6-week gap between the current and prior infections. A short course of
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is adequate treatment for lower tract infection in children.
(Choice B) Recurrent urinary tract infection can rarely be a sign of primary immunodeficiency; however, these patients have severe infections (ie,
pyelonephritis rather than cystitis) and multiple types of infections; this patient's medical history is otherwise unremarkable.
(Choice C) Sexual activity is associated with recurrent cystitis in women, but it is rarely the cause in children. The lack of genitalia injury to this
patient makes sexual abuse less likely; anal fissures are a common feature of chronic constipation.
(Choice E) An underlying anatomical condition (eg, vesicoureteral reflux) is a common cause of recurrent urinary tract infections in infants;
however, vesicoureteral reflux leads to recurrent upper (rather than lower) tract disease (ie, pyelonephritis).
Educational objective:
Chronic constipation is a risk factor for recurrent cystitis in young children. The impacted stool can cause rectal distension, which compresses the
bladder and urethra, prevents complete voiding, and leads to urinary stasis and bladder infection.

questions.prompt:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the office by his parents for a well-child check. This is the child's first appointment since the family purchased a new
house, and the parents want guidance on how to best child-proof the home. They moved into a single-story house built in 1985 in a quiet
neighborhood. Outside, there is an in-ground pool in the backyard and a private well used for drinking water. The father is a police officer and
keeps his handgun unloaded and inside a safe in the home office. There is an electric water heater, central air conditioning, and grounded
electrical outlets throughout the home. Which of the following is the best recommendation to provide safety for their child?

options.label: Install a 4-sided fence around the pool
Remove power outlets within the toddler's reach
Repaint the walls with lead-free paint
Set the water heater temperature to 60 C (140 F)
Store ammunition inside the safe with the handgun
Use bottled water exclusively for the child

questions.explanation:
Injury prevention in children
• Never leave child unattended around water
• Fence all 4 sides of pool & install self-locking, self-latching gate
Water
• Use life jackets
• Teach child to swim
• Install smoke detectors on every level of home
Fire
• Test smoke detectors & change batteries regularly
• If present, store guns unloaded and locked
Gun
• Store ammunition separately from guns
• Lock medications & toxic household products out of reach
• Remove dangling cords & cover power outlets
• Install safety gates on stairs
Home
• Set water heater to maximum temperature of 49 C (120 F)
• Mount furniture & TV to wall
• Avoid choking hazards (eg, whole grapes, raw vegetables, small objects)
Drowning is the number one cause of injury-related death in children age 1-4, and most cases involve home swimming pools. Anticipatory
guidance for water safety should be addressed at every well-child visit.
A fence is the most effective way to prevent drowning in a swimming pool by blocking unanticipated access. The fence should be ≥4 ft in height,
surround all 4 sides of the pool, and separate the pool from the yard and house. A child should not be able to fit through the slats or climb the
fence. Access to the pool should be through a self-closing gate that opens away from the pool and has a self-closing latch too high for a child
to reach. The gate should be locked when the pool is not in use. Gate alarms, pool alarms (which detect water movement), and pool covers may
also be used but not as a substitute for a fence. Children can drown by slipping under a pool cover or in water that has collected on top.
During any water activity (eg, pool, bath), a reliable supervising adult should be present and paying constant attention to children in water.
Other safety measures include swim lessons for children age ≥1, CPR training for parents, and life jackets (not "floaties" that may provide a false
sense of security). Parents should also ensure that safety measures are in place if visiting family or friends with pools.
(Choice B) Power outlets should be covered or blocked but do not need to be removed.
(Choice C) Lead-based paint was banned for use in houses in 1978; therefore, this house built in 1985 does not need to be repainted with lead-
free paint.
(Choice D) To prevent scalding injuries, the water heater temperature should be set to a maximum of 49 C (120 F).
(Choice E) Safe storage of a handgun includes keeping the gun unloaded and locked, with ammunition stored separately.
(Choice F) Well water may not contain adequate fluoride but is safe for drinking. Fluoride supplementation may be advised, but bottled water is
unnecessary and typically lacks fluoride.
Educational objective:
The most effective way to prevent children from drowning in swimming pools is to install a 4-sided fence around the pool with a self-closing gate
and latch. A reliable supervising adult should be present and paying constant attention to children during any water activity.

questions.explanation:
Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy)
• Insufficient dietary intake (lack of citrus fruits/vegetables)
• Chronic alcohol/substance use
Pathogenesis
• Severe malnutrition (eg, anorexia, restricted diet)
• Impaired collagen production
• Cutaneous:
• Coiled hair, perifollicular hemorrhages
• Petechiae, ecchymoses
Manifestations
• Impaired wound healing
• Mucosal: gingivitis with bleeding
• Musculoskeletal (eg, periosteal hemorrhage): arthralgia, limp
• Constitutional: malaise, depression, vasomotor instability
• Anemia (normocytic or microcytic)
Laboratory findings
• Normal platelet count & coagulation studies
• Oral/injectable vitamin C (improvement within days to weeks)
Treatment
• Toxicity (eg, abdominal pain, diarrhea) with excessive supplementation
This patient with a severely limited diet has leg pain, petechiae, and gingivitis, findings concerning for vitamin C deficiency (scurvy). This
condition is rare in resource-rich countries but can occur in patients who are malnourished; children with autism, as in this case, may have self-
restrictive diets that lack vitamin C-rich foods (eg, vegetables, citrus fruits), increasing the risk of deficiency.
Vitamin C is a cofactor for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine, which is essential for collagen cross-linking. Impaired collagen synthesis
compromises tensile strength, particularly in the skin and vascular walls, resulting in perifollicular hemorrhages, hemorrhagic gingivitis, petechiae,
and ecchymoses. Intramuscular or subperiosteal hemorrhages can occur, especially in the lower extremities due to gravity-dependent
hydrostatic pressure within fragile capillaries. This results in pain and difficulty with ambulation, which may be the presenting symptoms in
children, as seen here. Generalized malaise is also common.
The diagnosis can be confirmed by a low ascorbic acid level. Laboratory evaluation may also reveal anemia due to blood loss within tissues
(normocytic) or associated iron deficiency (microcytic, as in this case), the latter of which occurs in part because vitamin C normally enhances iron
absorption in the small intestine.

questions.prompt:
A 52-year-old man with a history of schizoaffective disorder is admitted to the hospital for treatment of a lower extremity cellulitis. The patient does
not appear to have any other acute medical illness. He is continued on his home medications-lithium, risperidone, and sertraline-and
cephalosporin therapy is initiated to treat his infection. During the hospital stay, the patient also receives ibuprofen and acetaminophen for pain
and lorazepam as needed for anxiety and insomnia. His infection improves over the next 10-14 days, but prior to discharge, he develops repeated
episodes of vomiting and diarrhea. At the same time, the patient becomes tremulous and uncoordinated, which makes it difficult for him to walk
without falling. In addition, he seems confused. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination shows fasciculations and bilateral tremor. Which of
the following medications is most likely to have caused this patient's new symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Lithium toxicity
Acute toxicity
• Intentional overdose
Chronic toxicity
Etiology
• Decreased renal perfusion (J lithium clearance)
• Dehydration
• Thiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors
Acute toxicity
• Gastrointestinal: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
• Late neurologic sequelae
Clinical features
Chronic toxicity (neurologic)
• Lethargy, confusion, agitation
• Ataxia, tremor/fasciculations, seizure
• Intravenous hydration
Treatment
• Hemodialysis (severe cases)
NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug.
The new onset of severe gastrointestinal symptoms, confusion, ataxia, and tremor (and other symptoms of neuromuscular irritability) in a
patient taking lithium suggests lithium toxicity. Lithium is a mood stabilizer used to treat bipolar disorder and schizoaffective disorder (bipolar
type). It has a narrow therapeutic index and relies on adequate kidney function for its excretion. This patient likely developed lithium toxicity due
to a drug interaction with ibuprofen. Concurrent use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (eg, ibuprofen) can cause a decrease in renal
clearance of lithium and lead to elevated serum lithium levels and lithium toxicity. Other drugs that increase lithium levels include thiazide
diuretics, ACE inhibitors, tetracyclines, and metronidazole.

effects such as ataxia, fasciculations, or tremor.
(Choice C) Lorazepam toxicity may cause sedation, confusion, and gait disturbance. However, it would not lead to fasciculations and bilateral
tremor. Alternatively, lorazepam withdrawal is unlikely to occur after 10-14 days of as-needed use.

• Hemodialysis (severe cases)

The new onset of severe gastrointestinal symptoms, confusion, ataxia, and tremor (and other symptoms of neuromuscular irritability) in a
patient taking lithium suggests lithium toxicity. Lithium is a mood stabilizer used to treat bipolar disorder and schizoaffective disorder (bipolar
type). It has a narrow therapeutic index and relies on adequate kidney function for its excretion. This patient likely developed lithium toxicity due
to a drug interaction with ibuprofen. Concurrent use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (eg, ibuprofen) can cause a decrease in renal
clearance of lithium and lead to elevated serum lithium levels and lithium toxicity. Other drugs that increase lithium levels include thiazide
diuretics, ACE inhibitors, tetracyclines, and metronidazole.
(Choice A) Acetaminophen may cause gastrointestinal symptoms and hepatic toxicity. However, it is not likely to cause adverse neurological
effects such as ataxia, fasciculations, or tremor.
(Choice C) Lorazepam toxicity may cause sedation, confusion, and gait disturbance. However, it would not lead to fasciculations and bilateral
tremor. Alternatively, lorazepam withdrawal is unlikely to occur after 10-14 days of as-needed use.
(Choice D) Risperidone, a second-generation antipsychotic, may cause galactorrhea, orthostasis, metabolic syndrome, and extrapyramidal
symptoms. Gastrointestinal symptoms are unlikely. In rare cases, risperidone can cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome, characterized by
autonomic instability, high fevers, delirium, and muscle rigidity.
(Choice E) Sertraline, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, may cause gastrointestinal symptoms, fasciculations, and tremor. However, it is
unlikely to lead to confusion or ataxia in therapeutic doses. If combined with other serotonergic drugs, it can lead to serotonin syndrome, which is
characterized by mental status changes, autonomic instability, hyperthermia, and neuromuscular irritability.
Educational objective:
The addition of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (or thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, tetracyclines, and metronidazole) to lithium can increase
serum lithium levels and lead to symptoms of toxicity, including gastrointestinal symptoms, confusion, ataxia, and tremor.

questions.prompt:
An 82-year-old man comes to the office for evaluation of a spot on his back. He thinks the skin lesion has been present for many months to a few
years but is unsure. The lesion was asymptomatic until it recently started itching; it is large and dark, but the patient is not sure whether it is
evolving. The spot is shown in the image below:
©UWorld
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient's skin lesion?

options.label: Punch biopsy from the lesion border
Punch biopsy from the lesion center

questions.explanation:
Clinical features of melanoma (ABCDE)
• Asymmetry: when bisected, the 2 sides are not identical
• Border irregularities: uneven edges, pigment fading off
• Color variegation: variable mixtures of brown, tan, black & red
• Diameter: ≥6 mm
• Evolving: lesion changing in size, shape, or color; new lesion
The initial clinical assessment of pigmented skin lesions should emphasize identifying those that could be melanoma and therefore warrant
biopsy. Biopsy is appropriate in any of the following situations:
• The lesion has features that suggest melanoma using a validated predictive rule (eg, lesions displaying ≥1-2 of the ABCDE criteria).
• The lesion has inflammatory changes; itching, crusting, or bleeding; or sensory changes (eg, paresthesia).
• The lesion is significantly different in appearance from other lesions on the same patient (ugly duckling sign).
• The lesion develops thickening or nodularity, which may indicate vertical growth and increase metastatic risk.
This patient's lesion is asymmetrical with a somewhat irregular border and notable color variegation (dark brown, light brown, and pink). The
associated itching further raises the risk, as does the apparent nodularity.
To rule out melanoma, full-thickness excisional biopsy with 1- to 3-mm margins of normal tissue is recommended. Partial excision (eg, deep
shave biopsy, central or peripheral punch biopsy) is generally only considered for very large lesions or lesions in locations where complete
excision may be problematic (eg, ear, face); partial excision may not allow adequate sampling for diagnosis or accurate measurement of the
lesion's depth (the most important prognostic indicator in melanoma) (Choices D and E).
(Choice A) In-situ destruction via cryotherapy or topical fluorouracil is indicated for treatment of actinic keratosis. Actinic keratosis presents as
small, roughened papules in sun-exposed areas (eg, scalp, face, hands) and typically is not pigmented.
(Choice C) Periodic surveillance is recommended for patients with numerous or atypical nevi that do not have suspicious features. Suspected
melanomas warrant tissue confirmation without delay.
Educational objective:
The assessment of pigmented skin lesions should include a predictive rule to estimate the risk of melanoma, such as the ABCDE (Asymmetry,
Border irregularities, Color variegation, Diameter, Evolving) rule; lesions with ≥1-2 of the ABCDE criteria warrant excisional biopsy. Biopsy is also
recommended for lesions with inflammation; itching, crusting, or bleeding; or sensory changes and for lesions that are significantly different in
appearance from other pigmented spots on the same patient (ugly duckling sign).

CSF = cerebrospinal fluid; ICP = intracranial pressure; IV = intravenous.
Premature infants are at increased risk of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). IVH can result in permanent obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
flow, resulting in persistent hydrocephalus. In these patients, a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is placed as a long-term solution to drain excess
CSF into the abdomen. Although it is a life-saving treatment, shunt malfunction (eg, catheter obstruction, shunt migration, split tubing) or
infection can result in rapid clinical decompensation due to recurrence of hydrocephalus.
This child has signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) including irritability, vomiting, and lethargy. In a patient with a VP shunt, the major
concern is shunt malfunction. Work-up focuses primarily on evaluating the patient's neurologic status (eg, neurologic examination, funduscopy),
the integrity of the shunt (eg, CT scan or ultrasound of the head, shunt series x-rays), and the possibility of infection (eg, complete blood count,
blood cultures, shunt tap).
Therefore, to evaluate for hydrocephalus due to shunt malfunction, urgent imaging with CT scan of the head or fast MRI of the brain should be
obtained. In addition, neuroimaging would also help to rule out other potential etiologies of increased ICP (eg, mass lesions).
(Choice A) Acetazolamide decreases CSF production and is used to treat idiopathic intracranial hypertension. However, this patient likely has
increased ICP due to obstructive hydrocephalus from shunt malfunction, so treatment would be aimed at restoring CSF drainage.
(Choice B) Empiric antibiotics are indicated for suspected device-associated ventriculitis but should ideally be initiated after CSF has been
obtained for cultures to guide therapy. This patient's lack of fever makes this diagnosis less likely, and neuroimaging should be performed first.
(Choice D) Electroencephalography is obtained for prolonged, unexplained, or recurrent seizures. A postictal state (usually <30 min) may cause
sleepiness, but this child has had symptoms for 24 hours with no history of abnormal movements.
(Choice E) Abnormal imaging in a patient with a VP shunt and signs of increased ICP typically warrants CSF evaluation via shunt aspiration.
Lumbar puncture is avoided in suspected obstructive hydrocephalus due to the potential of brain herniation (pressure difference between
ventricles and subarachnoid space).
Educational objective:
Signs of increased intracranial pressure (eg, irritability, vomiting, lethargy) in patients with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt should prompt urgent
evaluation for shunt complications (eg, infection, malfunction), including neurologic evaluation, CT scan of the head, and shunt series x-rays.

questions.prompt:
A 3-day-old boy is in the neonatal intensive care unit for management of prematurity. For the past hour, the patient has had decreased
spontaneous movements and tone. He has also had one episode of bradycardia and apnea. The patient was delivered vaginally at 28 weeks and
5 days gestation by a multiparous woman with cervical insufficiency. Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Birth weight
was 1.04 kg (2 lb 5 oz). Prenatal laboratory studies and ultrasounds were normal. Rupture of membranes occurred 3 hours prior to birth. The
amniotic fluid was clear, and there was no maternal fever. Temperature is 37.1 C (98.8 F). Head circumference is 28.5 cm, an increase of 3 cm
from yesterday. Examination shows a lethargic neonate with a weak cry, tense fontanelle, and generalized hypotonia. The patient then develops
a generalized seizure. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Intraventricular hemorrhage
• Rupture of fragile germinal matrix vessels
Pathophysiology
• Prematurity
Risk factors
• Very low birth weight
• Often asymptomatic
• Seizures or apnea
Clinical findings
• Full fontanelle
• Acute anemia
• Cranial ultrasonography*
Diagnosis
• Hyperechoic material (blood) within germinal matrix ‡ extension to ventricles or parenchyma
*Performed if symptomatic or as routine screening if <32 weeks gestational age.
This premature neonate with acute neurologic abnormalities and rapid increase in head circumference most likely has an intraventricular
hemorrhage (IVH). IVH is typically due to the rupture of germinal matrix vessels and can extend into the lateral ventricles. Premature
(specifically <32 weeks gestation) and very low birth-weight (<1500 g) newborns are at increased risk because their vasculature is fragile and
more susceptible to changes in cerebral perfusion (eg, hypotension, hypoxia, hypo- or hyperventilation).
IVH typically occurs in the first few days of life and is often asymptomatic. Symptomatic patients, such as this newborn, can have acute
neurologic changes (eg, lethargy, hypotonia, seizures). Hemorrhage may also cause anemia, a bulging fontanelle, a rapidly increasing head
circumference, bradycardia (eg, Cushing reflex), and apnea.
Cranial ultrasound is used to diagnose and grade IVH. Coagulated intraventricular blood has increased echogenicity compared with
cerebrospinal fluid filling a normal ventricle. Repeated scans are typically required to monitor progression of the bleed.
(Choices A and B) Hypocalcemia and hypoglycemia can cause lethargy, hypotonia, and seizure, but not a rapidly increasing head
circumference.
(Choice C) Hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is a global, anoxic cortical brain injury that occurs after severe perinatal asphyxia and
acidosis. This patient had normal Apgar scores and acute onset of neurologic abnormalities on day 3 of life, making HIE unlikely.
(Choice D) Inborn errors of metabolism (eg, maple syrup urine disease) are a rare cause of neonatal seizure, and a rapidly enlarging head
circumference makes IVH more likely.
(Choice F) Neonatal meningitis can present with nonspecific symptoms (eg, cardiopulmonary instability, neurologic decline). However, this
patient's normal temperature and lack of infectious risk factors (eg, maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes) make IVH more likely.
Educational objective:
Intraventricular hemorrhage is a common complication of prematurity and can present with acute neurologic changes (eg, seizure, apnea), a
bulging fontanelle, and a rapidly increasing head circumference.

questions.prompt:
A 16-year-old girl is brought to the office for evaluation of vulvar bumps. The bumps have been present for the past 4 months but are not painful
or itchy. She stopped shaving when she noticed that they were increasing in number and size. The patient is currently sexually active with one
partner, and she consistently uses condoms for contraception. BMI is 35 kg/m?. The lesions are shown in the exhibit. Which of the following
would have been most effective in preventing this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Genital warts (condylomata acuminata)
• HPV 6 & 11
Etiology
• Multiple pink or skin-colored lesions
Clinical features
• Lesions ranging from smooth, flattened papules
to exophytic/cauliflower-like growths
• Chemical: podophyllin resin, trichloroacetic acid
Treatment
• Immunologic: imiquimod
• Surgical: cryotherapy, laser therapy, excision
• Vaccination
Prevention
• Barrier contraception
HPV = human papillomavirus.
This patient has anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata) caused by low-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), typically types 6 and 11. HPV
enters the epidermis through sexual contact (ie, microabrasions), causing soft, fleshy, verrucous bumps that progress over several months.
Once present, anogenital warts can worsen or regress spontaneously (ie, immune clearance). Most patients are asymptomatic but some may
develop pruritus or friability (spotting with wiping).
HPV infection, particularly with high-risk types 16 and 18, is also associated with anogenital (eg, cervical, anal) and oropharyngeal cancers. The
most effective preventive strategy for both low-risk and high-risk types is HPV vaccination, ideally prior to initial sexual contact (ie, first HPV
exposure). Barrier contraceptive use is also protective (although skin contact beyond barrier protection may still permit viral transmission).
Small anogenital warts (ie, <1 cm) are treated with topical agents that can decrease wart size or induce regression by either chemical injury (eg,
trichloroacetic acid, podophyllin resin) or immunomodulation (eg, imiquimod). Surgical excision may be indicated for bulky, extensive lesions.
Recurrence rates are high regardless of treatment modality.
(Choice A) Pseudofolliculitis barbae (ie, "razor bumps") develop following hair removal, most often because of shaving. Inflamed follicular
papules develop in response to entrapped, recently trimmed hairs. This patient has verrucous, fleshy lesions from low-risk HPV infection instead
of inflamed papules related to shaving.

questions.prompt:
A 35-year-old man with schizophrenia is brought to the mental health clinic by his parents. They say that his prescription for risperidone ran out,
and they are worried because he is not sleeping well, is hardly eating, and has not showered for the past several weeks. The patient reluctantly
admits to hearing voices telling him to "do bad things." However, he becomes guarded and refuses to elaborate when asked to describe what the
voices say or whether he has followed their directives. The patient has a history of 4 psychiatric hospitalizations and a suicide attempt a year
ago. He lives with his elderly parents and is unemployed. On mental status examination, the patient is noted to be unkempt and malodorous. He
is highly anxious, makes no eye contact, and paces around the room. At one point, he whispers something while staring out the window. The
patient's speech is tangential and sometimes difficult to follow. When asked about suicidal or homicidal ideation, he shakes his head to indicate
"no." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?

options.label: Hospitalize the patient on an involuntary basis if necessary
Refill the prescription for risperidone and follow-up within 24 hours
Switch the patient to a risperidone long-acting injectable antipsychotic

questions.explanation:
Explanation
Although psychiatric treatment should take place in the least restrictive setting, safety considerations are paramount and require careful clinical
judgment. This acutely psychotic patient is experiencing command auditory hallucinations. His refusal to describe the voices apart from saying
that they are telling him to "do bad things" is concerning. The patient's history of multiple inpatient admissions suggests that he has a severe
course of illness, and his recent history of a suicide attempt is a risk factor for repeated suicidal behavior. He is not eating well or showering,
which indicates an inability to care for himself. This patient appears to be decompensating, making hospitalization the necessary course of action
for safety reasons.
Efforts should be made to hospitalize the patient voluntarily, but involuntary commitment should be implemented if he refuses. The legal
standards specifying the criteria for civil commitment vary by state, but they generally require the presence of a mental illness, danger to self or
others, and/or grave disability (inability to care for self) due to mental illness, as in this patient.
(Choices A and D) The patient should be restarted on risperidone as soon as possible, but it would be unsafe to treat him as an outpatient given
his current symptoms. Antipsychotics do not work immediately, and there is no way to know if he will take his medication or if his command
hallucinations will resolve within the next 24 hours. Clozapine can be considered in the management of treatment-resistant schizophrenia and is a
future option for this patient should his psychosis not be responsive to risperidone or another antipsychotic.
(Choice C) A urine drug screen (UDS) would be helpful in determining if substances are playing a role in the patient's decompensation. However,
the patient has a long history of psychotic illness and requires hospitalization, whether the UDS is positive or negative. In addition, obtaining a
urine sample, especially from someone who is agitated or confused, may take time and should not delay hospitalization.
(Choice E) Although converting the patient to a long-acting injectable (depot) antipsychotic would be a reasonable strategy to enhance
adherence, it is not an appropriate initial intervention. Conversion to a long-acting injectable formulation could be considered once the patient is
stabilized on oral antipsychotics in the hospital.
Educational objective:
Indications for psychiatric hospitalization include being a danger to self or others and/or grave disability. Hospitalization may be implemented on
an involuntary basis if necessary.

questions.prompt:
A 44-year-old man comes to the office due to depression, loss of interest, impaired concentration, fatigue, and poor sleep. The patient is not
suicidal and has no psychotic symptoms. He has no psychiatric history. Physical examination and laboratory evaluation are unremarkable. Major
depressive disorder is diagnosed, and he is treated with 50 mg of sertraline. After a month of antidepressant treatment, the patient reports
improvement in his energy level and sleep, although he continues to struggle with some sadness and low motivation. The dose of sertraline is
increased to 100 mg. At his 2-month follow-up, the patient has no depressive symptoms and says, "I feel like I'm totally back to normal. Work is
going well and I'm really enjoying life again.i He has no adverse effects from the sertraline. The patient asks when he can stop taking the
medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: Continue sertraline at a reduced dose for an additional 3 months
Continue sertraline for an additional 6 months
Continue sertraline for an additional 6 weeks
Gradually taper off sertraline over several weeks

questions.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has achieved remission after acute-phase treatment with sertraline. To decrease the risk of depressive relapse, multiple evidence-
based treatment guidelines recommend continuing antidepressant treatment for an additional 6 months in patients with remitted single-
episode, unipolar major depression (referred to as continuation-phase treatment). The dose should be maintained at the level at which
remission was achieved and should not be reduced (ie, the dose that gets the patient well keeps the patient well) (Choice A). If complete
remission is maintained at the end of the continuation phase, the antidepressant can then be tapered gradually and discontinued.
Maintenance-phase treatment is defined as continuing antidepressant medication past the initial continuation-phase treatment. Maintenance for 1-
3 years is appropriate for patients with a high risk of recurrence (eg, ≥2 episodes, persistent residual depressive symptoms) (Choice B). Patients
with a history of highly recurrent major depressive disorder (23 lifetime depressive episodes), chronic episodes (≥2 years), strong family history, or
severe episodes (eg, suicide attempt) should continue maintenance treatment indefinitely (Choice E).
(Choices D and F) Tapering and discontinuing sertraline now or in 6 weeks would increase the patient's risk for relapse. Sertraline should be
maintained for an additional 6 months to achieve sustained remission.
Educational objective:
Patients with a single episode of major depressive disorder should continue antidepressants for an additional 6 months following acute response
to reduce the risk of relapse. Patients with recurrent, chronic, or severe episodes should be considered for maintenance treatment (1-3 years or
indefinitely).

questions.prompt:
A 62-year-old man with hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease comes to the office due to uncomfortable, crawling sensations in his legs
that occur at night. The symptoms have been present daily for the past 2 months and start approximately 15-20 minutes after he gets in bed. He
can alleviate the symptoms by wiggling his legs or by getting up and walking, but the sensations return when he attempts to lie still again.
Physical examination shows no lower extremity sensory or motor abnormalities. Laboratory evaluation shows an elevated but stable creatinine

irresistible urge to move the legs when at rest. Symptoms occur primarily at night and are relieved by movement. RLS does not cause pain or
sensory deficits. The risk is increased in patients with chronic kidney disease.

Patients with low or low-normal serum ferritin levels (<75 ng/mL) should take supplemental iron. In addition, gabapentinoids (eg, gabapentin,
pregabalin), which are also called alpha-2-delta calcium channel ligands, are recommended for chronic, persistent symptoms. Gabapentin's
exact mechanism in improving RLS symptoms is unknown, but it affects A delta fibers, inhibits calcium influx, and blunts neurotransmitter release.
Dopamine agonists (eg, pramipexole, ropinirole) are also effective but can cause symptom augmentation (ie, paradoxical worsening) with daily,
long-term therapy and are no longer recommended as initial therapy for patients with chronic, persistent symptoms.
(Choice B) Benzodiazepines (eg, clonazepam) bind to GABA A receptors and enhance the inhibitory effect of GABA. Although benzodiazepines
are effective in RLS, the risk for tolerance makes other medications preferable for patients with daily symptoms. Gabapentin affects GABA activity
but does not directly target GABA A receptors.
(Choice C) Certain serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (eg, duloxetine) can treat neuropathic pain by modulating descending pain
pathways. Although peripheral neuropathy can cause discomfort in the feet, this patient's nocturnal symptoms, relief with walking, and normal
neurologic examination make RLS more likely.
(Choice D) Acetylcholine dysregulation may play a role in sleep-onset insomnia, which can be treated with dual orexin receptor antagonist
medications (eg, lemborexant). However, this patient's sleep disturbance is related to RLS rather than primary insomnia.
(Choice E) Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (eg, fluoxetine) inhibit presynaptic serotonin transporters, increasing the concentration of
serotonin within the synapse. They are used to treat depression, which can cause sleep disturbances, but are not indicated for RLS.

Restless legs syndrome is characterized by an uncomfortable urge to move the legs that is temporarily relieved by movement. Alpha-2-delta
calcium channel ligands (eg, gabapentin) are recommended as first-line therapy. Dopamine agonists (eg, pramipexole, ropinirole) are also
effective but can cause a paradoxical worsening of symptoms with long-term use.

questions.prompt:
A 15-year-old girl is brought to the office for evaluation of her menstrual periods. The patient underwent menarche at age 12 and initially had
irregular, heavy, nonpainful menses. Menses now occur monthly and consist of 4 days of light bleeding. For the past 3 months, the girl has
developed malaise and dizziness 2 days prior to her menstrual period and has had associated, continuous lower abdominal pain that radiates to
her thighs. Symptoms resolve on the second day of menses. She has no chronic medical conditions and takes no daily medications. The patient
is not sexually active. Her last menstrual period was a week ago. Vital signs are normal. The abdomen is soft, nontender, and nondistended and
has no palpable masses. Pelvic examination is deferred. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Primary dysmenorrhea
• Excessive prostaglandin production
Etiology
• Age <30
• BMI <20 kg/m2
• Tobacco use
Risk factors
• Menarche at age <12
• Heavy/long menstrual periods
• Sexual abuse
• Pain first 2-3 days of menses
Clinical features
• Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
• Normal pelvic examination
• Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Management
• Combination oral contraceptive pills
This adolescent's regular, painful menses after the establishment of ovulatory menstrual cycles is consistent with primary dysmenorrhea. During
menses, the endometrium produces and releases prostaglandins, stimulating uterine contractions and promoting endometrial sloughing. Patients
with primary dysmenorrhea have increased endometrial prostaglandin production, which causes uterine hypercontractility and hypertonicity
and resultant ischemia. Therefore, lower abdominal pain (which can radiate to the back and thighs) is typical, usually beginning 1 or 2 days prior
to menses (as uterine contractions initiate endometrial sloughing) and resolving a few days after onset of menses (as the endometrial lining thins).
Patients also often have associated malaise, dizziness, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Pelvic examination is normal and can be deferred in
patients who are not sexually active, as in this case.
First-line treatment in nonsexually active patients, such as this one, with primary dysmenorrhea is nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
because they inhibit prostaglandin synthesis. In sexually active patients, combination oral contraceptives are an option because they suppress
ovulation, providing contraception as well as decreasing prostaglandin release.
(Choice A) A copper-containing intrauterine device is not used for the treatment of primary dysmenorrhea because a common side effect of this is
painful, heavy menses.
(Choice B) Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists (eg, leuprolide) can be used in the treatment of endometriosis by suppressing ovulation. In
contrast to this patient, those with endometriosis have pain throughout the menstrual cycle and often have chronic pelvic pain.
(Choice D) Progestin-only pills are not as effective as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or combination oral contraceptives because they do
not decrease endometrial prostaglandin synthesis.
(Choice E) A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is first-line treatment in patients with premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and premenstrual
dysphoric disorder (PMDD). Although this patient has associated malaise, she does not have enough (5) systemic symptoms to meet PMS/PMDD
criteria.
(Choice F) Tranexamic acid is used in women who have heavy, regular bleeding and for whom combination oral contraceptives are
contraindicated (eg, thromboembolism). This patient has light bleeding.
Educational objective:
Primary dysmenorrhea occurs due to increased endometrial prostaglandin production during menses that causes uterine hypercontractility (eg,
crampy lower abdominal pain) and associated systemic symptoms (eg, malaise). First-line treatment is with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs,
which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis.

include hypertension, gout, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Cardiac monitoring shows atrial fibrillation at a rate of 120-140/min. His initial blood
pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. As the nurse attempts to establish intravenous access, the patient
becomes unresponsive. There is no palpable pulse over the carotids or femoral arteries, and he has agonal breathing. The cardiac monitor still
shows atrial fibrillation at the same rate. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
А. Arterial blood gas analysis
B. Chest compressions

IO = intraosseous; IV = intravenous; PEA = pulseless electrical activity; ROSC = return of spontaneous circulation;
VF = ventricular fibrillation; VT = ventricular tachycardia.
©UWorld
This patient is unresponsive and without a pulse, indicating sudden cardiac arrest (SCA). SCA management is based on 2 categories of
underlying cardiac rhythm:
• Pulseless electrical activity (PEA), seen in this patient, refers to an organized cardiac rhythm (eg, sinus bradycardia, atrial fibrillation) that
has become unable to generate sufficient cardiac output to create a measurable blood pressure or pulse (ie, nonperfusing). An underlying
mechanical issue (eg, severe hypovolemia, massive pulmonary embolism) or other potentially reversible cause (5 Hs and Ts) is typically
responsible, and the rhythm itself is unlikely the primary cause of SCA. Therefore, PEA is not a shockable rhythm; it is managed with
high-quality CPR (eg, chest compressions, epinephrine) and identification and treatment of potentially reversible causes (eg, volume
resuscitation, hypoxemia correction). PEA often degenerates into asystole (ie, complete absence of organized cardiac electrical activity),
managed the same as PEA.
• Ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT) represent instances in which the underlying rhythm is likely the primary
cause of SCA. Patients with VF/pulseless VT are managed with high-quality CPR and immediate defibrillation (ie, unsynchronized shock
with energy delivered randomly without synchronization to the QRS complex) (Choice C).
In contrast to defibrillation, synchronized cardioversion delivers a shock synchronized to the QRS complex. It can be used to attempt to restore
normal sinus rhythm in patients with a pulse who develop certain rapid cardiac arrhythmias, including symptomatic or sustained monomorphic VT
(unresponsive to antiarrhythmics) and hemodynamically unstable rapid atrial fibrillation. However, in patients without a pulse (eg, SCA due to
PEA), synchronized cardioversion is not appropriate regardless of the underlying cardiac rhythm (Choice E). Defibrillation would only be indicated
in VF/pulseless VT. In sum, there is no role for either defibrillation or synchronized cardioversion in PEA or asystole.
(Choice A) An arterial blood gas sometimes assists in recognizing an underlying cause of PEA (eg, severe acidemia) but should not delay
immediate initiation of chest compressions.
(Choice D) Intravenous epinephrine should be given every 3-5 minutes in the management of SCA. Intravenous lidocaine is sometimes given
after the third attempted defibrillation shock in SCA due to VF/pulseless VT, but intravenous amiodarone is typically preferred.
Educational objective:
Patients with sudden cardiac arrest should receive immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) with chest compressions. Pulseless electrical
activity/asystole is not a shockable rhythm and is managed with high-quality CPR and identification and treatment of potentially reversible causes.
*Amiodarone given after 3rd defibrillation shock.

questions.prompt:
A 54-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after sustaining severe burns from a deep fryer explosion that occurred when she
attempted to deep fry a frozen turkey. Temperature is 36 C (96.8 F). Blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg and pulse is 110/min. The patient is alert
but in severe pain. Examination reveals partial- to full-thickness burns of the face, neck, anterior chest and abdomen, and all 4 extremities.
Intravenous access is obtained, and crystalloid resuscitation is administered, along with analgesia. The patient is brought to the burn unit, where
her wounds are cleansed and dressed using topical antimicrobial ointment. During the subsequent treatment of this patient's burn injuries, which
of the following is most likely to decrease the patient's risk for developing infection?

options.label: Early initiation of total parenteral nutrition

questions.explanation:
Patients with severe burn injuries have multiple risk factors for wound infection and sepsis, including disruption of the skin's protective barrier,
burn-induced immunosuppression, and the presence of necrotic tissue (ie, burn eschar), which serves as an avascular, protein-rich substrate
for bacterial and fungal proliferation. To control the level of bacterial colonization on burned areas, topical antimicrobial agents are typically
applied during regular dressing changes. However, most topical agents cannot penetrate eschar, resulting in the eschar serving as a potential
nidus for infection.
Removal of eschar through early (eg, within 5 days of injury) wound excision and grafting reduces the risk of both noninvasive and invasive burn
wound infections.
• In the operating room, layers of devitalized tissue are progressively removed until capillary bleeding is encountered (ie, tangential excision).
• This is followed by application of split thickness skin grafts or, if graft donor sites are unavailable, other temporary coverage (eg, cadaveric
skin, manufactured skin substitutes).
Due to the high blood loss caused by excision and grafting, a series of smaller procedures is typically performed in patients with large body
surface area involvement.
(Choice A) Early nutritional support can offset hypermetabolism and improve overall outcomes in patients with severe burn injuries. However,
parenteral (ie, intravenous) nutrition is typically avoided because it is associated with higher rates of infection and mortality compared to enteral
(eg, via feeding tube) nutrition.
(Choice C) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy increases the plasma partial pressure of oxygen and is sometimes used to treat chronic, ischemic wounds
(eg, diabetic foot ulcers) or as an adjuvant treatment for severe soft tissue infections (eg, necrotizing fasciitis). However, increased plasma oxygen
levels cannot penetrate burn eschar because it is devascularized. Therefore, eschar removal is a better next step for both infection prevention (ie,
source control) and promotion of wound healing.
(Choice D) Even for severe burns, systemic antibiotics are not used prophylactically because they do not prevent burn sepsis (ie, invasive
infection) but instead may select for more aggressive, antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
(Choice E) Wound compression therapy can decrease hypertrophic scarring (rather than infection) in patients with severe burns. It is generally
used only after burned areas have fully healed, whether by epithelialization or skin graft adherence.
Educational objective:
In patients with severe burn injuries, early excision of necrotic tissue and wound closure (eg, skin grafting) reduces the risk of burn wound
infections.

questions.prompt:
A 46-year-old man is being evaluated for a gait disorder. He was referred by social workers due to frequent falls. His symptoms began gradually
about a year ago and have become progressively worse. The patient's history is notable for alcohol use disorder, and he is currently experiencing
homelessness, with sporadic stays in a nearby shelter. On examination, he has a broad-based, unsteady gait. A single tap on his patellar tendon
elicits persistent, slow, back-and-forth swinging of the leg. Nystagmus and truncal ataxia are also present. Which of the following additional
findings would most likely be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Alcoholic cerebellar degeneration
• >10 years heavy alcohol use
Epidemiology
• Degeneration of Purkinje cells (cerebellar vermis)
• Usually develops over weeks to months
• Wide-based gait
Manifestations
• Incoordination in legs
• Cognition usually intact
• Clinical:
• Impaired tandem walking/heel-knee-shin
Diagnosis
• Preserved finger-nose testing
• CT/MRI - cerebellar atrophy
• Alcohol cessation
Treatment
• Nutritional supplements
• Ambulatory assistance devices (eg, walker)
This patient has evidence of cerebellar dysfunction in the setting of likely alcoholic cerebellar degeneration. Typical features include
progressive gait dysfunction, truncal ataxia, and nystagmus. Patients often have evidence of postural incoordination (eg, inability to tandem
walk, abnormal heel-knee-shin testing) with relatively preserved limb coordination (normal finger-nose testing). Muscle hypotonia can also be
present, leading to a pendular knee reflex - persistent swinging movements of the limb after eliciting the deep-tendon reflex (more than 4 swings
is considered abnormal). Pendular reflexes are not brisk, unlike clonus, which would suggest pyramidal tract disease.
At later stages, patients may develop a postural tremor of the fingers and thighs, dysarthria, and visual problems (eg, diplopia).
(Choice A) A Babinski sign is an upward deviation of the great toe when the sole of the foot is stroked. It is evidence of hyperreflexia and
suggests an upper motor neuron lesion. It is not characteristic of cerebellar disease.
(Choice B) Bradykinesia, a general slowing of movement, is a hallmark of Parkinson disease. Parkinson disease is also characterized by resting
tremor, rigidity, and postural instability. Deep-tendon reflexes are generally normal.
(Choice C) The "clasp knife" phenomenon refers to a velocity-dependent resistance to passive movement of the limb. It is seen in patients with
hypertonia due to pyramidal tract disease and is not characteristic of cerebellar disease.
(Choice D) Thyroid disorders can affect deep-tendon reflexes and muscle tone, as well as general cognitive function. Specific features of
cerebellar dysfunction, such as ataxia or intention tremor, are uncommon.
(Choice E) Disorders affecting the inner ear and vestibulocochlear nerve can cause hearing loss and gait instability. The most common causes
include trauma, infection, and Ménière disease. Neoplasms of the cerebellopontine angle (eg, acoustic schwannoma) can cause cerebellar
dysfunction, vestibular dysfunction, and hearing loss. Alcoholic cerebellar degeneration, which is not associated with hearing loss, is more likely in
this patient.
Educational objective:
Cerebellar dysfunction is common among patients with alcohol use disorder. Manifestations include gait instability, truncal ataxia, and postural
incoordination.

questions.prompt:
A 32-year-old woman with bipolar disorder comes to the office for follow-up. The patient was diagnosed and treated for a manic episode at age 29
and has been stable on a combination of lithium and risperidone. Her mood has been "fine" overall, but she has been stressed about work. After
a staff meeting a few weeks ago, her supervisor said she appeared angry because she was repeatedly frowning while others were presenting.
Since then, the patient has been increasingly self-conscious and has started eating lunch alone at her desk. Temperature is 37.0 C (98.6 F), blood
pressure is 132/78 mm Hg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 14/min. Physical examination is unremarkable except for occasional grimacing
and slow inversion and tapping movements of her right foot. Lithium level is 0.9 mEq/L (normal: 0.6-1.2). Which of the following is the most
appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.label: Discontinue lithium and start valproic acid

questions.explanation:
Tardive dyskinesia
• Abnormal involuntary movements due to prolonged use of antipsychotics or metoclopramide

A complete hydatidiform mole (HM) is the result of abnormal fertilization of an empty ovum by either two sperms or one whose genome then
duplicates. The resulting gestation contains hypertrophic and hydropic trophoblastic villi that cause a marked elevation in the ß-hCG level. HM is
a premalignant disease that can develop into gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN), such as choriocarcinoma. B-hCG is secreted by all
gestational trophoblastic diseases (eg, hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma) and is therefore used as a marker for disease progression and/or
remission.

Acute pancreatitis
• Chronic alcohol use (~40%)
• Gallstones (~40%)
• Hypertriglyceridemia
Etiology
• Drugs (eg, azathioprine, valproic acid, thiazides)
• Infection (eg, CMV, Legionella, Aspergillus)
• latrogenic (post-ERCP, ischemic/atheroembolic)
Diagnosis (requires 2 of the following)
• Acute epigastric pain radiating to the back
• Amylase or lipase >3x normal limit
Clinical presentation
• Abnormalities on imaging consistent with pancreatitis
Other findings
• ALT level >150 U/L suggests biliary pancreatitis
• Severe disease: fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia, hypotension
ALT = alanine aminotransferase; CMV = cytomegalovirus; ERCP = endoscopic retrograde
cholangiopancreatography.
This patient has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and amylase/lipase levels >3 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), confirming the
diagnosis of acute pancreatitis.
In patients whose typical abdominal pain and markedly elevated amylase/lipase levels meet the diagnostic criteria for pancreatitis (such as this
one), CT scan is not required. In addition, if performed early (eg, within 72 hours of the onset of symptoms) CT scan is generally inaccurate for
grading disease severity since signs of impaired perfusion and/or necrosis typically take days to evolve. Therefore, CT scan is generally more
appropriate with diagnostic uncertainty or lack of improvement with conservative management of pancreatitis (Choice A).
Upon diagnosis of pancreatitis, an evaluation for potential causes should be performed. This patient does not use alcohol, takes no medications,
has normal triglyceride and calcium levels, and has had no recent major illness. Together with her high BMI, alanine aminotransferase >150
U/L, and elevated alkaline phosphatase all suggest gallstone pancreatitis. The best next step is a right upper quadrant (RUQ) ultrasound,
which is the most sensitive and specific test to detect the presence of gallstones. If gallstones are confirmed, cholecystectomy is indicated
following resolution of the acute pancreatitis episode.
(Choice B) Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan (cholescintigraphy) is used to diagnose acute cholecystitis if ultrasound does not provide
a clear diagnosis. It is not routinely used to evaluate pancreatitis.
(Choice C) A radiograph of the abdomen has very low sensitivity for gallstones since only a small percentage of gallstones contain sufficient
calcium to appear radiopaque on plain imaging.
(Choice E) Viruses (eg, hepatitis B, cytomegalovirus, varicella-zoster, HIV) are a less likely cause of pancreatitis in this patient. Serologic studies
can be deferred unless standard testing does not identify the cause.
(Choice F) Stool elastase is a marker for pancreatic exocrine function. Low levels would be seen in chronic, rather than acute, pancreatitis.
Educational objective:
Gallstone pancreatitis should be suspected in patients with pancreatitis (eg, epigastric pain, elevated amylase/lipase levels) who have risk factors
for gallstones and elevated liver function tests. Right upper quadrant ultrasound is the most sensitive and specific imaging study to detect
gallstones.

history of gout, which can present as acute inflammatory monoarthritis (with or without fever), his progressive symptoms over 3 days (gout flares
typically have an abrupt onset with maximal symptoms within 12-24 hr) increases the likelihood of a septic joint, considering his gout has been
previously well controlled. In addition, gout and other underlying joint disorders (eg, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis) or immunosuppressive
conditions (eg, diabetes mellitus) increase the risk for secondary joint infection.

questions.prompt:
A 77-year-old man comes to the office accompanied by his daughter due to "memory problems" and behavioral changes. The patient is a retired
accountant who lives alone and had been managing his finances and housework until a month ago. He says, "'ve had to ask my daughter to
shop for me and help around the house. I kept forgetting to turn off the stove and could have easily burned down the house." The patient has
been more tired than usual and sleeps through his favorite television shows. He previously maintained a rose garden but now feels "it's not worth
the effort." The patient's daughter says, "He was due for a medication refill last week but still has a few pills left because he sometimes forgets to
take them." Medical history includes hypothyroidism, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia. Temperature is 37.2 C (99 F), blood pressure is
141/87 mm Hg, pulse is 76/min, and respirations are 14/min. His weight is up 4 kg (8.8 lb) since last month. Physical examination, including
neurologic evaluation, is unremarkable. TSH is 3.7 uU/mL. He scores 21/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (normal: ≥26/30), with deficits
in delayed recall and attention. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's cognitive impairment?
questions.explanation:
Cognitive impairment in elderly patients
• Slight decrease in fluid intelligence (ability to process new information quickly)
Normal aging
• Normal functioning in all activities of daily living
• Mild decline in ≥1 cognitive domains
Mild neurocognitive disorder
(mild cognitive impairment)
• Normal functioning in all activities of daily living with compensation
• Significant decline in ≥1 cognitive domains
• Irreversible global cognitive impairment
Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia)
• Marked functional impairment
• Chronic & progressive, months to years
• Reversible mild-moderate cognitive impairment
Major depression
• Features of depression (mood, interest, energy)
• Episodic, weeks to months
In elderly patients, major depressive disorder (MDD) may be associated with significant cognitive impairment that can mimic a dementing
syndrome (eg, Alzheimer disease). This patient's anhedonia (eg, lack of interest in maintaining his rose garden because "it's not worth the effort"),
hypersomnia, low energy (eg, being more tired than usual, asking his daughter for help at home), weight gain, and impaired

Depression-related cognitive impairment (formerly "pseudodementia") is different than most other dementias in that it is reversible. Treatment

Although most women with hirsutism (excessive terminal hair growth) have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), rapid-onset hirsutism (eg, <1

due to an androgen-secreting neoplasm of the ovaries or adrenal glands.
The primary ovarian androgens are testosterone, androstenedione, and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). The adrenals also produce these
androgens as well as DHEA sulfate (DHEAS). Therefore, women with a suspected androgen-producing tumor should be evaluated with serum
testosterone and DHEAS levels:
• Elevated testosterone levels with normal DHEAS levels suggest an ovarian source (more common).
• Elevated DHEAS levels suggest an adrenal tumor (far less common).
DHEAS and DHEA have negligible intrinsic androgenic action but are converted to androstenedione and subsequently to testosterone in
peripheral tissues.

(Choice B) Imaging studies prior to biochemical confirmation of hyperandrogenism can be misleading because many patients have
nonfunctioning adrenal and ovarian masses that have no disease manifestations. If DHEAS levels are elevated, an abdominal CT scan is

(Choice C) Excessive body hair is common in women with acromegaly (elevated growth hormone increases insulin-like growth factor 1 levels).
However, hair growth is usually not rapidly progressive, and other clinical features of acromegaly (eg, enlarging facial features, macroglossia) are

common in patients with PCOS but is typically chronic and slowly progressive, beginning around puberty.

Rapid-onset hyperandrogenism, particularly with virilization, suggests an androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal neoplasm. Serum testosterone
and DHEAS levels are used to delineate the site of androgen production. Elevated testosterone with normal DHEAS suggests an ovarian source,
whereas elevated DHEAS suggests an adrenal source.
